0.title: Lamentations: Great Is Your Faithfulness
0.overview:
The message. Lamentations is what God’s people said, and prayed, standing in the ashes of Jerusalem. It tells the truth about three things at once: the LORD himself did this; he was right to do it, because his people had turned from him for generations; and it hurts beyond words. The book lets go of none of the three, and it never stops speaking to God. At its centre, at the lowest point, a broken man remembers who God is: “The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness” (3:22–23). So Lamentations teaches God’s people to grieve with faith, bringing their sorrow and their sin to the very God whose hand is heavy on them, because his mercy is the only hope there is.

Background: the disaster. For forty years Jeremiah had warned Judah that if it would not turn from its idols and injustice, the LORD would bring Babylon against it, but the people mocked God’s messengers “until there was no remedy” (2 Chronicles 36:16). In about 588 BC Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem, and for about eighteen months the city starved (2 Kings 25:1–3), until mothers ate their own children (4:10), as Moses had warned (Deuteronomy 28:53–57). In the summer of about 586 BC the wall was breached. King Zedekiah fled, was caught, saw his sons killed, and was blinded and taken to Babylon (2 Kings 25:4–7; Lamentations 4:20). The Babylonians burned the house of the LORD and every great house, broke down the walls and carried many into exile (2 Kings 25:8–11), while Edom, Judah’s brother nation, cheered (4:21; Psalm 137:7). The temple, the throne of David and the land, the visible signs that God was with his people, were all gone.

Background: the writer. The book does not name its author. From early times it has been linked with Jeremiah, who saw the siege, wept over his people (Jeremiah 9:1), and was himself thrown into a pit (Jeremiah 38:6), as the man of chapter 3 is (3:53). The Greek Old Testament adds a preface naming him; the Hebrew has none. Some scholars think the poems come from several hands, since the speakers of 4:17–20 once trusted a foreign nation and King Zedekiah, as Jeremiah never did; others answer that a poet speaking for the people voices what they felt. This commentary holds that the poems were most likely written by Jeremiah or someone close to him, an eyewitness, soon after the fall, while Mount Zion lay desolate (5:18) and before the exiles returned in about 538 BC. Nothing in the message hangs on the name: the poet speaks for the whole people.

The kind of writing. Lamentations is five poems of lament, one to a chapter. Chapters 1, 2 and 4 are acrostics: twenty-two verses, each beginning with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Chapter 3 gives three verses to each letter, which is why it has sixty-six. Chapter 5 keeps twenty-two verses but lets go of the alphabet. Grief is given the most ordered shape the poet has, as if this sorrow can be brought before God from A to Z. Several voices speak: a narrator, Jerusalem herself as a widow, a single afflicted man, and the whole community at prayer. Read it slowly, as prayer rather than argument.

How the book makes its case. Chapter 1 shows the city as a widow with “none to comfort her” (1:2), described by a narrator (1:1–11), then speaking herself (1:12–22): “The LORD is in the right, for I have rebelled against his word” (1:18). Chapter 2 sees the ruin from God’s side: the Lord “has done what he purposed; he has carried out his word, which he commanded long ago” (2:17), and the city is told to “pour out your heart like water before the presence of the Lord” (2:19). Chapter 3 is the heart of the book. One man speaks of God as his attacker until his hope is gone (3:1–18), calls to mind the LORD’s steadfast love (3:19–24), learns to wait quietly under God’s hand (3:25–39), calls the people to return (3:40–54), and hears the LORD say, “Do not fear!” (3:55–66). Chapter 4 returns to the siege and its guilty prophets and priests, and ends with the first clear word of hope: “The punishment of your iniquity, O daughter of Zion, is accomplished” (4:22). Chapter 5 is the people’s prayer, confessing “we have sinned!” (5:16) and looking up: “But you, O LORD, reign forever” (5:19). The hope stands at the centre, not the end; the book carries it back into the dark.

Did God really do this? Some readers soften the book: God only stood back and let Babylon do its worst. Lamentations will not allow that. The LORD did what he had warned he would do, and that is why his people can still speak to him and hope in him. Yet it also says he “does not afflict from his heart” (3:33), that the cruelty of those he used is evil, which “the Lord does not approve” (3:34–36), and that “the Lord will not cast off forever” (3:31). This commentary’s view is that God rules even over disaster without doing evil, and that the verdict here falls on a nation after centuries of warning. It is not a key to every sorrow: hard providences in a believer’s life are never in themselves a verdict on the sufferer. And the book ends without resolution: “Restore us to yourself, O LORD, that we may be restored! … unless you have utterly rejected us” (5:21–22). When Jews read it in the synagogue they repeat verse 21 after the last, so as not to close on despair. The poet leaves it open before God, and that too is faith: people who thought God had finished with them would not still be praying.

Where it leads: to Christ. Lamentations points to Christ by the need it exposes and the pattern of its suffering. Its ache is that Jerusalem has no comforter (1:2, 9, 16, 17, 21). God answered through Isaiah, “Comfort, comfort my people” (Isaiah 40:1), and in full in his Son, as “the Father of mercies and God of all comfort” (2 Corinthians 1:3). When Jesus came to the same city and “saw the city, he wept over it” (Luke 19:41). Jerusalem asked the passers-by, “Is it nothing to you?” (1:12); at the cross “those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads” (Matthew 27:39). The man of chapter 3, mocked and thrown into the pit, is a pattern of the one who suffered all of it with no sin of his own. Jerusalem drank the cup of the LORD’s anger for her own sins; Christ drank it for the sins of others, crying, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46). The punishment chapter 4 calls accomplished, he finished: “It is finished” (John 19:30). Because he was forsaken, no one who comes to him will be utterly rejected, and the tears no one wiped from Jerusalem’s cheeks, God himself will wipe away (Revelation 21:4).

For us. Lamentations gives the church permission to grieve. Lament is not unbelief; it is faith that keeps talking to God in the dark, telling him the truth about sin and pain together. It gives words to those who have lost homes, health, children or hope. It teaches us to “weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15) without hurrying them. And it shows where hope comes from when everything else has gone: not from a change of circumstances, for nothing outside has changed in chapter 3, but from what we call to mind about God. In Christ his mercies are new every morning, even here.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — How Lonely Sits the City
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jerusalem’s ruin is a reversal so complete that the poet can only cry “How”, and its cause is not Babylon but the LORD’s just response to her sin. The city once full of people sits alone like a widow, weeping at night with no one among all her lovers to comfort her (vv. 1–2). Judah has gone into exile and finds no rest, and the pilgrim roads mourn because no one comes to the feasts (vv. 3–4). Then the reason is named: “the LORD has afflicted her for the multitude of her transgressions” (v. 5). Her majesty is gone, her princes flee like starving deer, and she remembers the precious things of former days while her enemies mock (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: The first cause of Jerusalem's ruin is not Babylon's strength but the LORD's just response to her sin.

verseByVerse.quote: How lonely sits the city that was full of people! How like a widow has she become, she who was great among the nations! She who was a princess among the provinces has become a slave. She weeps bitterly in the night, with tears on her cheeks; among all her lovers she has none to comfort her; all her friends have dealt treacherously with her; they have become her enemies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The city that was full of life now sits alone like a widow, weeping through the night, and none of the allies she trusted will comfort her.

How lonely sits the city. The book opens with an exclamation, not an explanation. The crowds are dead or marched away (see the introduction), and the poet, standing in the ash, can only say: how.

Three reversals. Full of people, now lonely; great among the nations, now a widow; a princess, now a slave. The city sits, as mourners sat, on the ground with nowhere left to go.

How like a widow. In Israel a widow had lost her protector, her provider and her standing. But Jerusalem’s husband has not died; the LORD is alive. She is like a widow because the one who loved her has withdrawn his presence after she left him for others: the loneliness of a people whose God has stepped back.

She weeps bitterly in the night. Grief is worst at night, when there is nothing to do but feel it. One detail stays: “tears on her cheeks”, still there because no one has wiped them away.

Among all her lovers. Her lovers are the nations and their gods she ran after instead of the LORD: Egypt, Assyria and the alliances Jeremiah had warned would fail her (Jeremiah 2:36–37; 4:30). When the siege came, none of them came; the friends she trusted instead of God became her enemies.

None to comfort her. The chapter’s refrain sounds here for the first time and returns four more times (vv. 9, 16, 17, 21); the chapter does not hurry past it. Whatever you are grieving, it presses the right question: who is going to comfort me?

He will wipe away every tear. Lamentations does not reach the answer, but God had already given it. Through Isaiah he said, for this very ruin, “Comfort, comfort my people, says your God” (Isaiah 40:1), and “the reproach of your widowhood you will remember no more. For your Maker is your husband” (Isaiah 54:4–5). When the Son came, he wept over the same city (Luke 19:41), and the end of the Bible answers her tears in full: “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes” (Revelation 21:4).
verseByVerse.note: The book's Hebrew title is its first word, ekah, "How!" Jewish communities still read it on the ninth of Ab, the fast that mourns the destruction of the temple.

verseByVerse.quote: Judah has gone into exile because of affliction and hard servitude; she dwells now among the nations, but finds no resting place; her pursuers have all overtaken her in the midst of her distress. The roads to Zion mourn, for none come to the festival; all her gates are desolate; her priests groan; her virgins have been afflicted, and she herself suffers bitterly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah has been driven into exile with nowhere to rest, and the pilgrim roads to Zion stand empty, as Moses had warned would happen to a people that broke the covenant.

Judah has gone into exile. The people go out already broken by the siege, bent low under affliction and hard servitude (see the box below).

But finds no resting place. Moses had said exactly this would happen if Israel broke the covenant: “among these nations you shall find no respite, and there shall be no resting place for the sole of your foot” (Deuteronomy 28:65). The curses written centuries earlier are coming true.

Her pursuers have all overtaken her. So it was with the king. Zedekiah fled the city by night, and “the army of the Chaldeans pursued them and overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho” (Jeremiah 39:5).

The roads to Zion mourn. Picture the roads up to Jerusalem at the pilgrim feasts: families walking for days, singing as they climbed, the gates choked with crowds. “I was glad when they said to me, ‘Let us go to the house of the LORD!’” (Psalm 122:1). Now no one comes, and the poet says the roads themselves are in mourning.

All her gates are desolate. The gates where business was done and justice given are deserted, the priests have nothing to offer, and the young women who once danced at the feasts have been afflicted.

In everyday life. This city had grown used to the festivals and assumed they would always be there. It is possible to lose delight in God’s gathered people long before any building burns, and only notice what it was when the road is empty.

Uncertain wording. Two phrases here can be read more than one way, as the ESV margin notes. “Because of affliction” may also be rendered “under affliction”: Judah went into exile either because of the suffering of the siege or bent under it. And “in the midst of her distress” may be “in the narrow passes”, picturing fugitives trapped in a gorge with no way out. Either way, a people is driven out broken, with no escape.

Textual note. For “have been afflicted” the ESV notes that the Septuagint and Old Latin (ancient Greek and Latin translations) read “dragged away”.

verseByVerse.quote: Her foes have become the head; her enemies prosper, because the LORD has afflicted her for the multitude of her transgressions; her children have gone away, captives before the foe. From the daughter of Zion all her majesty has departed. Her princes have become like deer that find no pasture; they fled without strength before the pursuer. Jerusalem remembers in the days of her affliction and wandering all the precious things that were hers from days of old. When her people fell into the hand of the foe, and there was none to help her, her foes gloated over her; they mocked at her downfall.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem’s enemies have triumphed because the LORD himself afflicted her for her many sins, and now she remembers all she has lost while her foes laugh.

Her foes have become the head. Another covenant curse coming true: “He shall be the head, and you shall be the tail” (Deuteronomy 28:44).

Because the LORD has afflicted her. Mid-verse comes the reason, the conviction that holds the whole book together. The natural thing to say after a disaster is that the bigger army won. Lamentations will not say it. Babylon was the rod; the LORD held it, because of “the multitude of her transgressions”: not one sin but generations of idolatry, injustice and refusal to listen (Jeremiah 7:13).

The only ground for hope. Hard to hear, it is also the only ground for hope. If Babylon’s power were the last word, there would be nothing to pray for. If the LORD did this, the LORD can be spoken to, and the LORD can undo it.

The daughter of Zion. The city pictured as a young woman, a name that runs all through the book. Her princes are like starving deer, too weak to outrun anything. History stands behind the poetry: when the wall was breached, the king and his soldiers “fled, going out of the city at night by way of the king’s garden” (Jeremiah 39:4). The men who should have protected the people were the first out of the gate.

Jerusalem remembers. Memory is one of the cruellest parts of suffering. The worst nights are the ones when you remember what used to be: the house, the marriage, the health, the church, the child. A psalmist knew it: “These things I remember, as I pour out my soul: how I would go with the throng and lead them in procession to the house of God” (Psalm 42:4).

Remember something more. The poem goes no further yet. But keep a finger in this page: in chapter 3 the man who says “My soul continually remembers it and is bowed down within me” goes on: “But this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope” (3:20–21). The cure for a memory that drags you down is not to stop remembering but to remember something more: the steadfast love of the LORD, which is older than the good days and outlasts the bad ones.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sin does not only bring guilt; it defiles, exposes and blinds, and yet even here Jerusalem’s first words are a prayer. She “sinned grievously” and became unclean, her shame laid bare before those who once honoured her, because she never thought where her road would end (vv. 8–9). Her enemies seize the treasures of the temple and walk into the sanctuary where the nations were forbidden, while her people barter their valuables for bread (vv. 10–11). Twice she breaks into the narrator’s description with a cry that the LORD would simply look at her affliction (vv. 9, 11).
verseByVerse.theology: Sin blinds a people to its own future, but even in the ruin the first words spoken are addressed to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Jerusalem sinned grievously; therefore she became filthy; all who honored her despise her, for they have seen her nakedness; she herself groans and turns her face away. Her uncleanness was in her skirts; she took no thought of her future; therefore her fall is terrible; she has no comforter. "O LORD, behold my affliction, for the enemy has triumphed!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem’s sin has made her unclean and exposed her shame, because she never asked where her road would end; yet her first words are a prayer to the LORD.

Jerusalem sinned grievously. The narrator uses no softening. Sin is not only guilt before a judge; it defiles. It makes a person and a people unclean, and it cannot be hidden for ever.

They have seen her nakedness. Jeremiah had used this picture of public shame for the city that played the harlot with other gods: “I myself will lift up your skirts over your face, and your shame will be seen” (Jeremiah 13:26). The nations who once admired Jerusalem now see what she really is.

She herself groans and turns her face away. That is what shame does, and has done since the garden, where the first couple knew they were naked and hid from God (Genesis 3:7–10).

She took no thought of her future. The ESV margin gives “end”: she never thought where it would end. Moses had grieved over exactly this: “If they were wise, they would understand this; they would discern their latter end!” (Deuteronomy 32:29).

O LORD, behold my affliction. Then, for the first time, the city speaks, and her first words are a prayer. She has no comforter among the nations, so she turns to the only one left. Her pain has found the right address.

Clothing from someone else. The gospel’s answer to exposed shame is not a better hiding place but clothing from someone else: “white garments so that you may clothe yourself and the shame of your nakedness may not be seen” (Revelation 3:18). Christ was stripped at the cross so that we might be covered.

In everyday life. Sin is very good at the next five minutes and has nothing to say about the next five years, so it is wise to ask of any road, where does this end? But the strength to turn off it is not ours alone: the God who confronts Jerusalem here promised to put his Spirit within his people and cause them to walk in his ways (Ezekiel 36:27).

What it does not mean. This is a picture of a nation’s shame for its own unfaithfulness. It is never a word against anyone who has been stripped, exposed or abused by another person: that shame belongs to the one who did it, and anyone being abused should seek safety and help at once. God’s heart toward such victims is plain in 5:11, where their suffering is written into his book as an outrage.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “filthy” in verse 8 is rare. Many take it as a form of the word for ritual uncleanness that appears in verse 17; others connect it with a verb for shaking the head, so that she has become an object of scorn, or with a verb for wandering. Each fits the verse, since the next line says her admirers now despise her. The ESV’s “filthy” gives the likely sense.

verseByVerse.quote: The enemy has stretched out his hands over all her precious things; for she has seen the nations enter her sanctuary, those whom you forbade to enter your congregation. All her people groan as they search for bread; they trade their treasures for food to revive their strength. "Look, O LORD, and see, for I am despised."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pagan soldiers have walked into the holy place God had closed to them, the starving city trades its treasures for bread, and Jerusalem asks the LORD only to look.

She has seen the nations enter her sanctuary. The worst thing is not the looting of gold but who is standing where. The law barred certain peoples from the assembly of the LORD (Deuteronomy 23:3), and the holy place was closed to all but the priests. Now pagan soldiers walk into it and carry out its vessels.

Those whom you forbade. Mid-sentence the description turns into prayer: Lord, you made the rule; look who is in your house.

They trade their treasures for food. The siege ended in famine: “the famine was so severe in the city that there was no food for the people of the land” (Jeremiah 52:6). Heirlooms, jewellery and the family’s savings were all handed over for a loaf. The treasures Jerusalem had trusted turned out to be worth one meal.

Look, O LORD, and see. Twice now the city has asked God simply to look, not yet to fix it: the most basic prayer there is, and he hears it. “You have kept count of my tossings; put my tears in your bottle” (Psalm 56:8).

Not as invaders but as guests. The gospel turns the irony inside out. The nations did come into God’s house, in a way no one in Jerusalem could have imagined. Jesus spoke of “the temple of his body”, destroyed and raised in three days (John 2:19–21), and through that temple outsiders are brought in, not as invaders but as guests: “you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:13).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–16 — Is It Nothing to You?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now Jerusalem speaks for herself, and she traces every blow to the hand of the LORD. She stops the travellers on the road and asks whether her sorrow means nothing to them (v. 12). In picture after picture, fire in the bones, a hunter’s net, a yoke made of her own sins, an army summoned, grapes trodden in a winepress, she says what God has done to her in his fierce anger (vv. 13–15). Then she comes back to the loss that hurts most: “a comforter is far from me, one to revive my spirit” (v. 16). Christians have long heard these words again at the cross.
verseByVerse.theology: Zion’s sorrow came from the LORD’s anger against her own sin; the sorrow of Christ, which these words have long been used to describe, came from the LORD’s anger against ours.

verseByVerse.quote: "Is it nothing to you, all you who pass by? Look and see if there is any sorrow like my sorrow, which was brought upon me, which the LORD inflicted on the day of his fierce anger. "From on high he sent fire; into my bones he made it descend; he spread a net for my feet; he turned me back; he has left me stunned, faint all the day long.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem calls on the passers-by to see that no sorrow is like hers, because it is the LORD who has struck her in his fierce anger.

Is it nothing to you, all you who pass by? Now the city herself stands by the roadside and calls to travellers who walk past a catastrophe and carry on with their day. Her question has a plain first meaning: suffering is lonelier when others treat it as background, and there is a sin of the passer-by, to see someone’s ruin and feel nothing. The church is meant to be the place where no one’s sorrow is nothing to anyone (2 Corinthians 1:4).

From on high he sent fire. Four pictures, and he is the subject of every one: fire from above, a hunter’s net, a traveller turned back on the road, a body left stunned and fainting.

Into my bones he made it descend. Jeremiah once said God’s word was “a burning fire shut up in my bones” (Jeremiah 20:9). The city refused that fire, so it received the other kind. The word of God will burn in you one way or the other: as a message you cannot keep in, or as a judgment you cannot keep out.

Those who passed by derided him. Christians have long heard verse 12 at the foot of the cross, with good reason. At Golgotha “those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads” (Matthew 27:39), and there, by the road outside Jerusalem, a man suffered what this verse describes, the LORD’s fierce anger. Yet look at the difference, because it is the whole gospel. Jerusalem’s sorrow came “for the multitude of her transgressions” (v. 5); she says so herself (v. 18). Christ had none: “he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities” (Isaiah 53:5). Jerusalem drank the cup of wrath for her own sin; Jesus drank it for ours. Is there any sorrow like his sorrow? No, because his was the only sorrow ever borne entirely for someone else.

Scrolling past the ruins. No generation has seen more suffering than ours, and perhaps none has found it easier to pass by. A war, a flood or a famine arrives on the same screen as a recipe and a joke, and the thumb moves on. We are not monsters; there is simply too much, and the mind protects itself by turning catastrophe into content, something to watch rather than something that happens to people. Jerusalem’s question cuts through: she asks the traveller not to defeat Babylon, only to stop and look. Yet guilt about scrolling is no cure; a heart cannot be shamed into compassion. What turns spectators into neighbours is being loved by someone who did not pass by. On the road to Jericho a priest and a Levite saw the wounded man and kept walking, and the Samaritan “came to where he was” (Luke 10:33). Behind that story stands its teller, who came much further, down into our ruin at his own cost. Those he has lifted out of the ditch find it harder and harder to walk past anyone else’s.

verseByVerse.quote: "My transgressions were bound into a yoke; by his hand they were fastened together; they were set upon my neck; he caused my strength to fail; the Lord gave me into the hands of those whom I cannot withstand. "The Lord rejected all my mighty men in my midst; he summoned an assembly against me to crush my young men; the Lord has trodden as in a winepress the virgin daughter of Judah. "For these things I weep; my eyes flow with tears; for a comforter is far from me, one to revive my spirit; my children are desolate, for the enemy has prevailed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem’s own sins have become a yoke on her neck, the Lord has crushed her strength like grapes in a winepress, and what she needs most, a comforter, is far away.

My transgressions were bound into a yoke. Each sin was like a strap. One by one they were fastened together into a yoke and laid on her neck until she could not stand up under it (see the box below). That is how sin feels when it is finally felt: nobody notices one strap, but one day the whole weight arrives at once.

He summoned an assembly against me. The word is the one used for Israel’s appointed feasts. God has called a gathering, not of worshippers to a festival but of an army to a slaughter (compare 2:22).

As in a winepress. Grapes were trampled by foot in a winepress until the juice ran red. It is a terrible picture of judgment, and the New Testament keeps it for the end of history: “the great winepress of the wrath of God” (Revelation 14:19). What Judah felt in 586 BC was a foretaste of a day still to come for the whole world, which is why the refuge from that day is not a strong city but a Saviour.

One to revive my spirit. She names exactly what she needs: not an explanation or a lecture, but someone to come near and revive her spirit.

Take my yoke upon you. Then hear another yoke: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you … For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:28–30). Jesus does not invite people with no yoke. He invites people bent double under the one they tied themselves, and offers to exchange it. And he answered her other hunger on the night before he died: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, to be with you forever … I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you” (John 14:16, 18). The comforter who was far from Jerusalem has come near in the Son, and dwells in his people by his Spirit.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the meaning of the Hebrew in the first line of verse 14 is uncertain. The verb rendered “were bound” is very rare, and the ancient translations read the line in different ways. The ESV’s picture, sins fastened together into a yoke by the Lord’s hand, is the most widely accepted sense, and it fits what follows: the weight on her neck makes her strength fail.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–22 — The LORD Is in the Right
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Grief that confesses God is right can still pour itself out to him and ask him for justice. The narrator pictures Zion with her hands stretched out and no one to take them, her neighbours turned enemies at the LORD’s command (v. 17). Then she speaks the heart of the chapter: “The LORD is in the right, for I have rebelled against his word” (v. 18). The allies she trusted deceived her, and her leaders died searching for food (v. 19). She lays her distress before God, admits her rebellion, and asks him to deal with her gloating enemies as he has dealt with her (vv. 20–22). The poem ends there, with no comforter and no answer yet.
verseByVerse.theology: Grief that confesses God is right can still pour itself out to him, and ask him for justice.

verseByVerse.quote: Zion stretches out her hands, but there is none to comfort her; the LORD has commanded against Jacob that his neighbors should be his foes; Jerusalem has become a filthy thing among them. "The LORD is in the right, for I have rebelled against his word; but hear, all you peoples, and see my suffering; my young women and my young men have gone into captivity. "I called to my lovers, but they deceived me; my priests and elders perished in the city, while they sought food to revive their strength.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With no one to take her outstretched hands, Jerusalem confesses that the LORD is in the right and she is the rebel, and asks the nations to learn from her suffering.

Zion stretches out her hands. The narrator breaks in for a single verse, like a camera pulling back: hands stretched out in pleading, and no one to take them.

His neighbors should be his foes. Even her neighbours’ hostility is traced to the LORD: he commanded it. And she has become “a filthy thing among them”, the thing people step around. The Hebrew word is the one the law used for the uncleanness of a woman’s monthly flow (Leviticus 15:19–24), which kept a person from the sanctuary for a time. Jerusalem, meant to be the place of God’s presence and a light to the nations, is now the thing they keep away from.

The LORD is in the right. Verse 18 carries the whole book. In the worst pain she has ever known, Jerusalem does not accuse God. She accuses herself: “for I have rebelled against his word”. That shapes how the whole book prays. It is full of raw, loud, honest complaint, but it is the complaint of someone who has first agreed with God about her sin. Paul says the same of every human being: “Let God be true though every one were a liar” (Romans 3:4).

But hear, all you peoples. She asks the nations to learn from her. Her ruin is meant as a warning (1 Kings 9:8–9): the same end awaits any people that forsakes the LORD.

I called to my lovers, but they deceived me. She called on Egypt, and Egypt did not come (Jeremiah 37:7); her priests and elders died scavenging for food. What she trusted instead of God failed her when she needed it.

Two ways of suffering. One way of suffering says, “I have done nothing to deserve this,” and ends in bitterness. The other says, “God is right, and I am hurting, and I am going to tell him both,” and that way leads home, because the God who is in the right is the God who forgives the one who confesses (Psalm 32:5; 1 John 1:9).

What it does not mean. Jerusalem makes this confession as a nation under the covenant curse, after generations of warning. It does not make every sorrow a sign of some particular sin: hard providences in a believer’s life are never in themselves a verdict on the sufferer (see the introduction). What the verse teaches every sufferer is to agree with God about whatever sin he does show us, and to keep speaking to him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Look, O LORD, for I am in distress; my stomach churns; my heart is wrung within me, because I have been very rebellious. In the street the sword bereaves; in the house it is like death. "They heard my groaning, yet there is no one to comfort me. All my enemies have heard of my trouble; they are glad that you have done it. You have brought the day you announced; now let them be as I am. "Let all their evildoing come before you, and deal with them as you have dealt with me because of all my transgressions; for my groans are many, and my heart is faint."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem lays her anguish and her rebellion before the LORD together, and asks him to bring on her gloating enemies the same day of reckoning he has brought on her.

My heart is wrung within me. The prayer turns fully to God, and it is physical: a churning stomach, a heart wrung like a cloth. Grief lives in the body as well as the mind, and Scripture is not embarrassed to say so (Psalm 31:9–10).

Because I have been very rebellious. Again the double honesty: “I am in distress” and “I have been very rebellious”. She does not use her pain to excuse her sin, or her sin to silence her pain.

In the street the sword bereaves. Outside, the sword; inside, famine and disease. There is nowhere safe to stand.

You have brought the day you announced. The prophets had announced the day of judgment for years, and it came. Still with no one to comfort her (the refrain’s fifth and last sounding), she asks for its other half: “now let them be as I am.”

Is this a right prayer? It is not a prayer for private revenge. It asks God to be consistent, to deal with the evil of the nations as he has dealt with the evil of his own people. And God answered it; of Babylon he said, “repay her according to her deeds” (Jeremiah 50:29). Christians may pray in the same way, but we have been shown more. We leave vengeance with God (“never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God”, Romans 12:19), and we have heard the one who bore that wrath pray, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34).

The chapter simply stops. It ends with no resolution and no comforter. Lamentations lets that stand, and so should we when we sit with someone in grief: do not hurry them to the last page. But the comforter she looked for has a name. “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matthew 5:4).

Textual note. The ESV notes two places where ancient translations read differently. For “They heard my groaning” the Septuagint and Syriac read “Hear”, making the line a plea for God to listen. For “You have brought the day” the Syriac reads “Bring”, a prayer that the LORD will bring the same day on her enemies.

1.title: The City with No Comforter
1.overview:
Where we are. Lamentations opens in the ashes. Jerusalem has fallen to Babylon, and this first of five poems, an alphabetic acrostic (see the introduction), looks at the ruined city as a widow weeping through the night.

The message. The LORD has done this, he was right to do it, and it hurts beyond words. Jerusalem’s ruin is not Babylon’s victory but God’s just answer to generations of sin, and the city confesses it: “The LORD is in the right, for I have rebelled against his word” (v. 18). Yet confession does not silence her. She brings her pain to the very God whose hand is on her, and the chapter shows that this is what faith does in the dark.

Why it was said. The first hearers were survivors, among the ruins or in exile, asking whether God had abandoned them and whether he had been fair. The poem gave them words to tell the truth about their sin and their sorrow at once, and to say both to God.

How the chapter makes its case. A narrator speaks first. The city sits lonely, betrayed by her lovers, her pilgrim roads empty, and the cause is named: “the LORD has afflicted her for the multitude of her transgressions” (vv. 1–7). Her sin has made her unclean and exposed; enemies walk into the sanctuary, and twice she breaks in to ask the LORD to look (vv. 8–11). Then Jerusalem speaks, stopping the passers-by and tracing every blow to the LORD’s hand (vv. 12–16). Finally she confesses that the LORD is in the right, pours out her anguish and asks him to deal with her enemies as he has dealt with her (vv. 17–22). Five times the refrain sounds, “none to comfort”, and the chapter ends without an answer.

Where it leads. To Christ, by the need the chapter exposes and the pattern of its suffering. The comforter Jerusalem cannot find is the one God promised through Isaiah and sent in his Son, who wept over the same city (Luke 19:41) and promised his people “another Helper” (John 14:16). Her cry, “Is it nothing to you, all you who pass by?” (v. 12), was heard again at the cross, where “those who passed by derided him” (Matthew 27:39). But there is a difference that is the whole gospel: Jerusalem bore the LORD’s anger for her own transgressions; Christ bore it for ours.

For us. This chapter gives grieving people permission to weep and words to pray. It teaches us to agree with God about our sin without hiding our pain from him, to take our sorrow to him first, and to stop for those whose ruin others walk past. And it points us to the Comforter she lacked, who is near to all who mourn.
1.theology:
The LORD, not Babylon, is the first cause of Jerusalem's ruin, and he acted justly; the covenant curses were fulfilled to the letter (vv. 3, 5, 18; Deut 28:44, 65). Sin defiles as well as condemns, blinds a people to where its road will end, and binds itself together into a yoke too heavy to carry (vv. 8-9, 14; Deut 32:29).

Yet the chapter is also a school of lament. Jerusalem agrees with God about her sin and still pours out her pain to him, asking first only that he would look (vv. 9, 11, 18, 20). That is faith, not unbelief. The comforter she cannot find is the deepest wound of the chapter, and God answers it in Christ, who bore the LORD's anger for the sins of others, and in the Spirit he sends (v. 12; Isa 40:1; Isa 53:5; Matt 27:39; John 14:16-18; 2 Cor 1:3-4).
1.examples:
Anyone who has lain awake after a death knows the picture of verse 2: weeping in the night, when there is nothing to do but feel it, with tears still on the cheeks because no one is there to wipe them away. Lamentations does not tell such a person to cheer up. It gives them words, and turns those words towards God.

The passer-by of verse 12 is also familiar. When a friend's life falls apart, it is easy to walk past their ruin and get on with the day. The church is meant to be the place where no one's sorrow is nothing to anyone.

keyVerse.quote: The LORD is in the right, for I have rebelled against his word; but hear, all you peoples, and see my suffering; my young women and my young men have gone into captivity.
keyVerse.note: This verse is the hinge of the chapter and of the way the whole book prays. In the middle of unbearable loss Jerusalem does not accuse God; she agrees with him about her sin, and then asks the world to see her pain. Honest confession and honest grief stand side by side, both spoken before the God who is in the right and who forgives those who confess.

1.reflection:
Jerusalem’s deepest wound is that she has “none to comfort her” (vv. 2, 9, 16, 17, 21). When you have grieved, what made comfort hard to find, and what kind of presence actually helped?

Verse 5 says the LORD afflicted the city “for the multitude of her transgressions”, and in verse 18 she confesses that he is in the right. How can we take this seriously without turning every sorrow, our own or someone else’s, into a verdict on the sufferer?

Jerusalem’s “lovers”, the allies she trusted instead of God, failed her when she needed them most (vv. 2, 19). What do people around you lean on for safety instead of God, and where do you feel the same pull?

“Is it nothing to you, all you who pass by?” (v. 12). Whose suffering is easiest for you to walk past, and how does Jesus, who did not pass by, change the way you see them?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The Day of His Anger
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The ruin of Jerusalem was the Lord’s own work, and the poet will not soften it; nearly every verb has the Lord as its subject. In his anger he has covered Zion with a cloud, thrown down her splendour and forgotten his own footstool, the temple (v. 1). He has swallowed up Jacob without mercy, torn down its strongholds and humbled its kingdom (v. 2), and withdrawn the right hand that once saved Israel (v. 3). He has bent his bow against his own people and poured out his fury like fire, until the poet says it outright: “The Lord has become like an enemy” (vv. 4–5).
verseByVerse.theology: God's anger is not an impersonal force but the personal opposition of a holy God to sin.

verseByVerse.quote: How the Lord in his anger has set the daughter of Zion under a cloud! He has cast down from heaven to earth the splendor of Israel; he has not remembered his footstool in the day of his anger. The Lord has swallowed up without mercy all the habitations of Jacob; in his wrath he has broken down the strongholds of the daughter of Judah; he has brought down to the ground in dishonor the kingdom and its rulers. He has cut down in fierce anger all the might of Israel; he has withdrawn from them his right hand in the face of the enemy; he has burned like a flaming fire in Jacob, consuming all around.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In his anger the Lord himself has thrown down Zion’s glory, forgotten his own temple and withdrawn the hand that used to save her.

From God’s side. Chapter 1 kept close to the city and her grief; chapter 2 turns its eyes to God. Count the subjects of the verbs in the first eight verses: nearly every one is the Lord.

Under a cloud. In Israel’s story the cloud meant glory: “the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle” (Exodus 40:34); at the temple’s dedication it drove the priests out (1 Kings 8:10–11). Now the cloud over Zion is anger (see the box below).

His footstool. The ark and the temple where it stood, the place where heaven’s King rested his feet on earth (1 Chronicles 28:2; Psalm 99:5). The people assumed God would never let anything happen to it (Jeremiah 7:4). He did not remember it. No sacred place shelters from God people who will not turn to him.

Without mercy. The phrase returns as “without pity” (vv. 17, 21), and the whole book turns on the moment the same poet says “his mercies never come to an end” (3:22). In chapter 2 mercy is withheld; in chapter 3 the poet finds that it was never exhausted.

He has withdrawn from them his right hand. Israel had sung of that right hand since the Red Sea: “your right hand, O LORD, shatters the enemy” (Exodus 15:6). Now it is withdrawn, and Judah faces Babylon alone. One way God judges is not to strike but to step back and leave people to what they chose.

Uncertain wording. The verb translated “set … under a cloud” occurs nowhere else in the Old Testament. Most connect it with the Hebrew word for cloud, as the ESV does; a few link it with a word meaning to disgrace. The ESV’s reading is the likely one.

verseByVerse.quote: He has bent his bow like an enemy, with his right hand set like a foe; and he has killed all who were delightful in our eyes; in the tent of the daughter of Zion, he has poured out his fury like fire. The Lord has become like an enemy; he has swallowed up Israel; he has swallowed up all its palaces; he has laid in ruins its strongholds, and he has multiplied in the daughter of Judah mourning and lamentation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord has turned his weapons on his own people and stands against them as an enemy would.

The Lord has become like an enemy. Everything hangs on the small word “like”. God has not become a different God or stopped being in covenant with Israel. But in what he is doing he stands against them exactly as an enemy would, bow bent and arrow aimed.

He has poured out his fury. Modern people often want a God who can be disappointed but never angry. Lamentations will not allow it. God’s wrath is not a loss of temper but the settled, personal opposition of perfect holiness to evil, which is why Scripture says “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” (Hebrews 10:31).

Jesus drank it in full. Now bring those words to the cross. Paul says we were the enemies: “while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son” (Romans 5:10). And at the cross the Son himself cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46). Enemies of God become his friends only because his Son bore what it is to have God against you. What Jerusalem experienced in part, Jesus drank in full, so that no one who is in him will ever have to say, “The Lord has become like an enemy.”

What it does not mean. A Christian in deep trouble may feel that God has become like an enemy, and may tell him so, as this poet does. But for those who are in Christ the feeling is not the verdict: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–10 — Festival, Sabbath, King and Priest
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When a people keeps up the outward acts of worship but refuses the God they worship, he may take those acts away. The LORD tears down his own temple as easily as a harvest shelter, ends festival and Sabbath, and spurns king and priest (v. 6). He scorns his altar, and the enemy shouts in his house as worshippers once shouted at the feasts (v. 7). He measures the walls for demolition (v. 8); the gates sink, the king is in exile, the law is no more, and the prophets have no vision (v. 9). From elders to young women, the whole city sits on the ground in dust and sackcloth (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: When a people keeps up the outward acts of worship but refuses the God they worship, he may take those acts away.

verseByVerse.quote: He has laid waste his booth like a garden, laid in ruins his meeting place; the LORD has made Zion forget festival and Sabbath, and in his fierce indignation has spurned king and priest. The Lord has scorned his altar, disowned his sanctuary; he has delivered into the hand of the enemy the walls of her palaces; they raised a clamor in the house of the LORD as on the day of festival.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD has torn down his own temple and spurned the festivals, king, priest and altar that Judah treated as guarantees.

He has laid waste his booth like a garden. A booth was a flimsy harvest shelter in a vineyard or garden, taken down when the harvest was over. Isaiah had pictured the daughter of Zion “left like a booth in a vineyard” (Isaiah 1:8). The temple of Solomon, seven years in the building, came down as easily as a harvest hut.

Festival and Sabbath, king and priest. With it went the whole shape of Israel’s life with God: the calendar of feasts and Sabbath, the throne and the altar. All were gifts; Judah had treated them as guarantees.

As on the day of festival. The temple is loud again, with the wrong noise: soldiers shouting in triumph where the choirs used to sing.

Why would God scorn his own altar? Because the people kept up the sacrifices while living in rebellion. Jeremiah had stood in the temple gate and asked, “Has this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes?” (Jeremiah 7:11), and centuries later Jesus quoted those words in the temple courts (Matthew 21:13). Here is a question for every churchgoer: do I treat worship as a way to meet God, or as insurance against having to obey him?

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD determined to lay in ruins the wall of the daughter of Zion; he stretched out the measuring line; he did not restrain his hand from destroying; he caused rampart and wall to lament; they languished together. Her gates have sunk into the ground; he has ruined and broken her bars; her king and princes are among the nations; the law is no more, and her prophets find no vision from the LORD. The elders of the daughter of Zion sit on the ground in silence; they have thrown dust on their heads and put on sackcloth; the young women of Jerusalem have bowed their heads to the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD planned the city’s destruction with a builder’s care and took away king, law and prophetic word, leaving everyone sitting in the dust.

He stretched out the measuring line. Builders measure before they build; this measuring is for demolition, just as deliberate. God had said so through his prophets in Manasseh’s day: “I will stretch over Jerusalem the measuring line of Samaria” (2 Kings 21:13). The fall of the city was no accident of war.

The law is no more. Worse than the broken gates is the silence. With no priests left to teach the law and no temple to keep it, “her prophets find no vision from the LORD”. Amos had warned of “a famine … of hearing the words of the LORD” (Amos 8:11), and a psalm that mourns the burning of the sanctuary says, “there is no longer any prophet” (Psalm 74:9).

The elders of the daughter of Zion sit on the ground. From the oldest to the youngest, the whole city is on the ground, and the elders who used to give counsel at the gate have nothing to say. Dust on the head and coarse sackcloth were the ordinary signs of mourning in Israel, worn for the dead and in national disaster (Genesis 37:34; Joshua 7:6; Job 2:12).

The Word came. The silence of verse 9 did not last. God spoke again through the prophets of the exile, and at last “in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son” (Hebrews 1:2), the Word made flesh (John 1:14). The law that was no more, he fulfilled; the vision the prophets could not find, he is.

In everyday life. A people that refuses God’s word for long enough may find it withdrawn. Do not assume that a Bible on the shelf and a sermon every Sunday will always be there for when you are finally ready to listen. While he still speaks, his word is an open door: “Seek the LORD while he may be found” (Isaiah 55:6). And sometimes silence and dust are the only honest response; the church should know how to sit on the ground with the grieving before it knows what to say to them.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Prophets who hide sin cannot heal, and behind all the sorrow stands the LORD who kept his word. The poet’s composure breaks: he weeps as children faint for hunger and die in their mothers’ arms, and he can find nothing to compare with a ruin “vast as the sea” (vv. 11–13). The prophets had flattered instead of exposing sin (v. 14); now passers-by mock the city once called “the perfection of beauty” (v. 15), and her enemies boast that they have swallowed her (v. 16). But the true cause is none of these: “The LORD has done what he purposed; he has carried out his word, which he commanded long ago” (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Prophets who hide sin cannot heal, and the God who kept his word in judgment keeps it in mercy too.

verseByVerse.quote: My eyes are spent with weeping; my stomach churns; my bile is poured out to the ground because of the destruction of the daughter of my people, because infants and babies faint in the streets of the city. They cry to their mothers, "Where is bread and wine?" as they faint like a wounded man in the streets of the city, as their life is poured out on their mothers' bosom. What can I say for you, to what compare you, O daughter of Jerusalem? What can I liken to you, that I may comfort you, O virgin daughter of Zion? For your ruin is vast as the sea; who can heal you?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The poet is undone as little children die of hunger in their mothers’ arms, before a ruin so vast that only God can heal it.

My eyes are spent with weeping. The narrator has been describing; now he weeps. It is the voice of the prophet who said, “Oh that my head were waters, and my eyes a fountain of tears” (Jeremiah 9:1). “My bile” is literally “my liver”: the inner organs stood for the deepest feelings, and his are poured out on the ground.

Infants and babies faint in the streets. The detail is almost unbearable, and meant to be. Little children ask the question they asked every day, “Where is bread and wine?”, and their mothers have nothing to give. They die in their mothers’ arms, and the poet does not hurry past them. Sin is never only private; its consequences fall even on the most innocent.

What can I say for you? The poet wants to comfort and cannot find the words; every comparison is too small for a ruin “vast as the sea”. “Who can heal you?” has only one answer. The God who struck is the only one who can heal: “For I will restore health to you, and your wounds I will heal, declares the LORD” (Jeremiah 30:17).

Theology with tears. The man who most clearly says God did this is the man most undone by it. Anyone who speaks of God’s judgment without tears has not understood it. Jesus himself, approaching the city he knew would be destroyed, “saw the city, he wept over it” (Luke 19:41). And the Healer came in person: “with his wounds we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5).

For grieving parents. If you have lost a child, hear this carefully. The poet does not say these children died for their own sins, or that their mothers failed them; he weeps for them. The God who wrote their cry into Scripture is the God Jesus showed when he took children in his arms and blessed them (Mark 10:16). The Westminster Confession speaks of the little ones God has chosen who die in infancy as saved by Christ through his Spirit (chapter 10, section 3), and David could say of his dead son, “I shall go to him” (2 Samuel 12:23).

verseByVerse.quote: Your prophets have seen for you false and deceptive visions; they have not exposed your iniquity to restore your fortunes, but have seen for you oracles that are false and misleading. All who pass along the way clap their hands at you; they hiss and wag their heads at the daughter of Jerusalem: "Is this the city that was called the perfection of beauty, the joy of all the earth?" All your enemies rail against you; they hiss, they gnash their teeth, they cry: "We have swallowed her! Ah, this is the day we longed for; now we have it; we see it!" The LORD has done what he purposed; he has carried out his word, which he commanded long ago; he has thrown down without pity; he has made the enemy rejoice over you and exalted the might of your foes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
False prophets soothed the city instead of exposing her sin, and now her enemies gloat; but the real cause of her ruin is the LORD, doing exactly what he said he would do.

Your prophets have seen for you false and deceptive visions. Here is the tragedy behind the tragedy: the prophets told those who stubbornly followed their own hearts, “No disaster shall come upon you” (Jeremiah 23:17).

To restore your fortunes. Exposing her iniquity would have been the kind thing, because it was the road to restoration. Their smooth words felt like love and ended in famine.

The perfection of beauty. The city’s own songs are thrown back at her. The psalms had called Zion “the perfection of beauty” (Psalm 50:2) and “the joy of all the earth” (Psalm 48:2). Now travellers clap, hiss and wag their heads, and quote them as a joke.

We have swallowed her! The enemies take the credit, but the poet has twice said who did the swallowing (vv. 2, 5). They think it is their day. It is the LORD’s.

The LORD has done what he purposed. The deepest cause was not the false prophets, the enemy or chance. The word he “commanded long ago” is the covenant warning of Moses, spelled out in Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28. This is terrifying, and also the firmest ground of hope in the chapter: a God who keeps his word to the letter in judgment will keep it to the letter in mercy. The same chapter of Leviticus that warned of the siege also said, “Yet for all that, when they are in the land of their enemies, I will not spurn them, neither will I abhor them so as to destroy them utterly and break my covenant with them” (Leviticus 26:44).

He stood where ruined Jerusalem stood. The gestures of verse 15 are the ones the Gospels record at the cross: “those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads” (Mark 15:29; Psalm 22:7). The Son of God stood where ruined Jerusalem stood, mocked and apparently abandoned, though he had done nothing to deserve it.

In everyday life. This is searching for every preacher, parent and friend: “Faithful are the wounds of a friend” (Proverbs 27:6). And for every listener: “people will not endure sound teaching, but having itching ears they will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own passions” (2 Timothy 4:3). Which kind of voice do you want in your life?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–22 — Pour Out Your Heart Like Water
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The right response to God’s judgment is not silence or flight but prayer that holds nothing back. The poet urges the city to weep day and night and give itself no rest (v. 18), to “pour out your heart like water before the presence of the Lord”, and to lift its hands for its dying children (v. 19). Then the city prays, boldly. She asks the LORD to look and remember who these people are to him, and she names the worst horrors of the siege: mothers eating their children, priests killed in the sanctuary, young and old dead in the streets (vv. 20–21). The chapter ends with a mother’s cry and no answer yet (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: The fitting response to God's judgment is not silence or flight but prayer that holds nothing back.

verseByVerse.quote: Their heart cried to the Lord. O wall of the daughter of Zion, let tears stream down like a torrent day and night! Give yourself no rest, your eyes no respite! "Arise, cry out in the night, at the beginning of the night watches! Pour out your heart like water before the presence of the Lord! Lift your hands to him for the lives of your children, who faint for hunger at the head of every street."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The poet calls the ruined city to pour out her whole heart before the Lord without rest, and to lift her hands for her starving children.

Their heart cried to the Lord. The people who ignored him so long are now calling on him, and the poet urges them not to stop. Even the city wall is told to weep (see the box below).

Before the presence of the Lord. Look where they are told to take their grief: not away from God, but before the very Lord who has done this. The one who wounded is the only one who can bind up (Hosea 6:1).

Pour out your heart like water. Poured-out water cannot be gathered back and tidied up, and that is the prayer God invites: “Trust in him at all times, O people; pour out your heart before him” (Psalm 62:8). You do not need to arrange your feelings before you pray. Bring them as they are.

For the lives of your children. When parents cannot feed, protect or fix, they can still lift their hands to God for their children. That is not the least a parent can do; it is the most.

The way in is open. Christ himself “offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears” (Hebrews 5:7), and now he is the high priest who is able “to sympathize with our weaknesses”, so that we may “with confidence draw near to the throne of grace” (Hebrews 4:15–16).

How do I pour out my heart? Lamentations is the pattern. Go to him first. At 2 a.m., before the phone or the fridge, say the first true sentence to God, even if it is only “Look, O LORD, and see” (1:11). Say it all. Name the loss, the fear and the anger in your own words, aloud or on paper, without dressing it up; this poet takes five chapters to do it. Say it to him, not only about him. Complaint to friends goes round in circles; complaint to God goes somewhere. Keep at it. “Arise, cry out in the night” (v. 19), and again the next night if need be.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 18 reads “Their heart cried to the Lord” without saying whose heart, then turns suddenly to address the wall. The ESV keeps it as it stands, taking “their” as the survivors; several modern translations, by a slight change to the Hebrew, read a command to the wall itself to cry aloud to the Lord. Either way, the call is to unceasing prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: Look, O LORD, and see! With whom have you dealt thus? Should women eat the fruit of their womb, the children of their tender care? Should priest and prophet be killed in the sanctuary of the Lord? In the dust of the streets lie the young and the old; my young women and my young men have fallen by the sword; you have killed them in the day of your anger, slaughtering without pity. You summoned as if to a festival day my terrors on every side, and on the day of the anger of the LORD no one escaped or survived; those whom I held and raised my enemy destroyed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The city lays the worst horrors of the siege before the LORD and boldly asks him to remember who these people are to him.

With whom have you dealt thus? The prayer is shockingly bold: Lord, these are your people; remember who we are to you. This is the argument Moses used on the mountain when God’s wrath burned against Israel (Exodus 32:11–12). It is not rebellion to remind God of his covenant. It is faith taking hold of the only claim it has.

Should women eat the fruit of their womb? The horror she names is the one Moses had foretold for a siege: “you shall eat the fruit of your womb, the flesh of your sons and daughters” (Deuteronomy 28:53). It came true. And priests and prophets were killed in the sanctuary they trusted to keep them safe.

You have killed them. She says it to God’s face. Scripture includes prayers like this because God would rather have our honest anguish than our polite distance.

My terrors on every side. This was Jeremiah’s own phrase (Jeremiah 6:25), and his enemies once whispered it back at him in mockery (Jeremiah 20:10). Now it has come. God summoned the terrors as people were once summoned to a feast.

Those whom I held and raised. The chapter ends with a mother’s cry, and no answer yet. Jesus, walking to his own death, told the women of Jerusalem, “do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children” (Luke 23:28), because he knew another such day was coming to the city that rejected him. The only shelter from “the day of the anger of the LORD” is the one who went into that day on our behalf.

Did mothers really eat their children? Yes. It was foretold as the covenant curse (Deuteronomy 28:53–57) and had happened in an earlier siege (2 Kings 6:28–29). Scripture records it to show what sin and judgment truly are, and that God hears even that cry.

How should such a verse be read? With tears, and without contempt for those mothers. The poet lays the horror before God as the deepest wound of the siege and asks him to look. For anyone who has seen, suffered or even done unspeakable things under extreme pressure, the verse says that these too may be spoken before the Lord, and that there is a Saviour whose blood cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7). Memories like these should not be carried alone. A pastor or biblical counsellor and trusted friends are part of God’s care, and so is a doctor where sleep, appetite or daily life have been overwhelmed; taking that help is no failure of faith.

2.title: The Lord Has Become Like an Enemy
2.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 showed Jerusalem as a weeping widow with no one to comfort her. The second poem, another acrostic, looks at the same ruin from God’s side, and does not flinch.

The message. The destruction of Jerusalem was the Lord’s own deliberate work. He became like an enemy to his people, tore down his own temple and took away king, priest, law and prophet, because he “has carried out his word, which he commanded long ago” (v. 17). Holy places gave no shelter to a people who refused him. Yet the right response is not to run from this God but to “pour out your heart like water before the presence of the Lord” (v. 19), because the God who kept his word in judgment is the only one who can heal.

Why it was said. Their prophets had told them Jerusalem could never fall while the LORD’s temple stood in it (Jeremiah 7:4; see the introduction). Now the temple was ash, and the survivors needed to know who had done this, why, and whether they could still pray to him.

How the chapter makes its case. The Lord in his anger has swallowed up Jacob and become like an enemy (vv. 1–5). He has wrecked his own sanctuary, measured the walls for demolition, and silenced law and vision (vv. 6–10). The poet’s composure breaks as children die in their mothers’ arms, flattering prophets are exposed and passers-by mock; but behind it all, “The LORD has done what he purposed” (vv. 11–17). Finally he urges the city to cry out day and night, and she does, laying the siege’s horrors before the LORD (vv. 18–22).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the need the chapter exposes and the character of God revealed in him. Here the Lord is “like an enemy” to his own people, and on the day of his anger “no one escaped or survived” (vv. 5, 22). At the cross the Son of God entered that day himself, mocked by passers-by (Matthew 27:39) and crying, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46), so that God’s enemies might be reconciled to him (Romans 5:10). The God who kept his word of judgment to the letter has kept his word of mercy in his Son.

For us. Do not treat church or a Christian upbringing as insurance against listening to God, and value those who tell you the truth about your sin. When grief or guilt overwhelms you, do not run from God: pour out your heart before him and lift your hands for your children, for in Christ the way into his presence is open.
2.theology:
God's wrath is personal: in judgment the Lord acts like an enemy toward his own people (vv. 4-5). His anger is holy, deliberate and measured, not a loss of control (vv. 8, 17; Heb 10:31).

Sacred places and religious practices do not protect people who refuse God himself; he may scorn his own altar (vv. 1, 6-7; Jer 7:4, 11).

God can withdraw his word from those who will not hear it (v. 9; Amos 8:11). Prophets who do not expose sin cannot bring restoration (v. 14; Prov 27:6; 2 Tim 4:3).

God kept his word when he carried out the judgments he had warned of, so he will also keep his promises of mercy (v. 17; Lev 26:44-45).

The right response to God's judgment is honest, persistent prayer poured out before him, including a bold reminder that they are his own people (vv. 18-20; Ps 62:8; Exod 32:11-12).

Christ bore God’s anger against sinners so that his enemies might be made his friends (Rom 5:10; Matt 27:46), and he wept over the city that would reject him (Luke 19:41).
2.examples:
The poem's pictures stay with a reader: the cloud of glory turned into a cloud of anger, the right hand that once shattered enemies simply withdrawn, and Solomon's temple coming down like a harvest shelter, measured out for demolition.

Hardest of all is a child asking for bread and wine and dying in his mother's arms, while prophets who never mentioned sin are exposed and the old songs about Zion are quoted back as a joke. The poem does not answer with an explanation but with a prayer: a heart poured out like water that cannot be gathered up again, asking, With whom have you dealt thus?

keyVerse.quote: The LORD has done what he purposed; he has carried out his word, which he commanded long ago; he has thrown down without pity; he has made the enemy rejoice over you and exalted the might of your foes.
keyVerse.note: This verse names the true cause of everything in the chapter: not Babylon’s strength or the false prophets’ lies, but the LORD carrying out the covenant warning he gave through Moses. It is terrifying, and it is also the ground of hope, for a God who keeps his word to the letter in judgment will keep his promises of mercy too. That is why the next verses can tell the city to pour out her heart before him (v. 19).

2.reflection:
Chapter 2 insists again and again that the Lord himself did this (vv. 1–8, 17). Why do you think the poet will not soften it, and how can it become a ground of hope rather than only of fear?

Judah trusted the temple, the festivals and the king to keep them safe (vv. 1, 6–7). What religious habits or Christian privileges are we tempted to treat as insurance against having to listen to God?

The false prophets “have not exposed your iniquity to restore your fortunes” (v. 14). Who in your life tells you the truth, and how do you receive it? How can we speak hard truth to others in love?

The city is told to “pour out your heart like water before the presence of the Lord” (v. 19). What holds you back from praying like that, and how does Jesus, who prayed “with loud cries and tears” (Hebrews 5:7), give you confidence to do it?
