verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — The Man Who Has Seen Affliction
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A believer may come to the point of saying that his hope is gone, and still be saying it to the LORD. One man now steps forward and speaks of God as his attacker: he has seen affliction “under the rod of his wrath” and been driven into darkness without light (vv. 1–3). His body wastes, he is walled in and his prayers seem shut out (vv. 4–9). God seems a bear in ambush and an archer taking aim (vv. 10–13), his own people laugh at him and bitterness is his only food (vv. 14–16). At last he says the bleakest thing in the book: “My endurance has perished; so has my hope from the LORD” (vv. 17–18).
verseByVerse.theology: A believer may reach the point of saying his hope is gone, and still be saying it to the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: I am the man who has seen affliction under the rod of his wrath; he has driven and brought me into darkness without any light; surely against me he turns his hand again and again the whole day long.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A single man steps forward and says that God himself has been his attacker, driving him into utter darkness and striking him again and again. The first two poems spoke about a city; now the whole book narrows to one person’s suffering.

I am the man. He does not give his name. His experience is so close to Jeremiah’s, mocked by his own people and thrown into a pit (v. 53), that many have heard the prophet’s voice here (see the introduction). But he speaks as one who carries the nation’s grief in his own body, so that anyone who has suffered can stand where he stands. He has “seen” affliction, lived inside it, “under the rod of his wrath”.

Without any light. Not a dim room but no lamp at all: no sense of direction, no way to see where the next step goes. Many believers know such a season, and Isaiah wrote for them: “Let him who walks in darkness and has no light trust in the name of the LORD and rely on his God” (Isaiah 50:10).

Again and again the whole day long. One blow can be survived. What wears a person down is blow after blow with no gap to breathe: the diagnosis, then the job loss, then the family crisis. And he feels singled out: “against me”.

verseByVerse.quote: He has made my flesh and my skin waste away; he has broken my bones; he has besieged and enveloped me with bitterness and tribulation; he has made me dwell in darkness like the dead of long ago.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His suffering is in his body as well as his soul: God has worn away his flesh, besieged him with bitterness and laid him in darkness like the long-forgotten dead.

My flesh and my skin. Skin, flesh, bones: the famine and siege wrote themselves on the body. Scripture never treats the body as unimportant to God, nor bodily pain as unspiritual.

He has broken my bones. Yet the God who breaks bones mends them. David, crushed by his own sin, prayed, “let the bones that you have broken rejoice” (Psalm 51:8): the hand that broke is the hand he asked to heal.

He has besieged and enveloped me. An army had walled in Jerusalem; now he says God has done that to him personally, surrounding him with “bitterness and tribulation”, so that every way he turns he meets it.

Like the dead of long ago. Not just dying, but like the long-forgotten dead whom no one visits. A psalmist said the same, “You have put me in the depths of the pit, in the regions dark and deep” (Psalm 88:6), and that psalm ends in darkness too. God has put such prayers in his book so that no sufferer will ever think his darkness too dark to bring to him.

verseByVerse.quote: He has walled me about so that I cannot escape; he has made my chains heavy; though I call and cry for help, he shuts out my prayer; he has blocked my ways with blocks of stones; he has made my paths crooked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He feels imprisoned by God, and worst of all, his loud prayers seem to be shut out.

He has walled me about. Walls, chains, blocked roads and crooked paths: a prisoner with no way out and no way forward. Job used the same picture: “He has walled up my way, so that I cannot pass” (Job 19:8).

He shuts out my prayer. Cruellest of all, he is praying, loudly (“I call and cry for help”), and God seems to shut the prayer out as someone shuts a door.

When prayer seems unanswered. Christians sometimes say that God always answers prayer. That is true, but it is not how it always feels, and this verse gives permission to say so. Hold on to this line, though, for at the end of the chapter the same man says, “you heard my plea” (v. 56): the door was not locked forever. And the Son of God, “in the days of his flesh”, offered up “prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears”, and “he was heard” (Hebrews 5:7), so that through him no believer’s prayer is ever truly shut out.

verseByVerse.quote: He is a bear lying in wait for me, a lion in hiding; he turned aside my steps and tore me to pieces; he has made me desolate; he bent his bow and set me as a target for his arrow. He drove into my kidneys the arrows of his quiver;
verseByVerse.commentary:
God seems to him like a bear in ambush and an archer taking aim, and he is the prey and the target. The pictures are violent because affliction feels violent, yet the God who tears means to heal.

A bear lying in wait for me. God is a bear waiting in ambush, a lion crouched in the undergrowth; the man walks into the trap and is torn to pieces.

He bent his bow and set me as a target. He feels like the target on an archery range, every arrow finding its mark and driven deep into “my kidneys”, the inmost parts. Job said the same: “he set me up as his target; his archers surround me” (Job 16:12–13).

He tears that he may heal. Hosea used the same picture and drew a surprising conclusion: “Come, let us return to the LORD; for he has torn us, that he may heal us; he has struck us down, and he will bind us up” (Hosea 6:1). A lion tears to kill; God tears to heal. The wound is real, but its purpose is return, not destruction.

How can a believer speak of God like this? Because it is honest about how affliction feels, and because the Bible itself uses these images for God’s judgment (Hosea 5:14). The man is not saying God is cruel. He is saying God is not safe to trifle with, which is exactly what Judah forgot.

For the believer who feels targeted. You are not the first believer to feel that God has made you his target. And the Son of God, who truly stood under the arrows of God’s wrath at the cross, felt it most of all, not for his sins but for ours.

verseByVerse.quote: I have become the laughingstock of all my people, the object of their taunts all day long. He has filled me with bitterness; he has sated me with wormwood. He has made my teeth grind on gravel, and made me cower in ashes;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mocked by his own people and fed on nothing but bitterness, he is humiliated and in pain at once.

The laughingstock of all my people. The mockery is public and constant, and because it comes from “my people”, those who should have stood with him, the wound is deeper. Jeremiah knew exactly this: “I have become a laughingstock all the day; everyone mocks me” (Jeremiah 20:7).

He has sated me with wormwood. Wormwood was a plant with an intensely bitter taste, and it became a byword for bitterness in life. To be “sated” with it is to have eaten nothing else, bitterness as your whole diet.

My teeth grind on gravel. Bread full of grit, so that every mouthful hurts. And he is pressed down into the ashes of his burned city, the place where mourners sat.

Jesus was a laughingstock too. He was mocked by the soldiers who knelt before him and cried, “Hail, King of the Jews!” (Matthew 27:29), and he bore it without one word of reviling.

Uncertain wording. The verb translated “made me cower” occurs only here in the Old Testament. It seems to mean to press down or trample, so the picture is of being pushed face down into the ashes; older translations guessed ‘covered me with ashes’. Either way he lies humiliated in the ruin.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read ‘all peoples’ instead of “all my people”. Either way the mockery is public, but “my people” makes it more painful.

verseByVerse.quote: my soul is bereft of peace; I have forgotten what happiness is; so I say, "My endurance has perished; so has my hope from the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the bottom of the pit he says that his strength and his hope from the LORD are gone, yet even here he names the LORD.

My soul is bereft of peace. Peace has been taken from him like a family member taken by death. The ESV notes that the Hebrew behind “happiness” is ‘good’: he has forgotten what good is. In a few verses the same man will say “good” three times over (vv. 25–27). He does not relearn the good by looking at his circumstances, but by looking at God.

My endurance has perished. This is the bottom: he cannot keep going, and he no longer expects anything from God. Elijah said something like it under the broom tree: “It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life” (1 Kings 19:4).

My hope from the LORD. Yet even at the bottom he names the LORD. A person who has truly let go of God does not grieve the loss of hope in God. The very ache of this verse shows that faith is not dead, only exhausted, and the next verses show what exhausted faith does next.

He has been this low. In Gethsemane the Lord Jesus said, “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death” (Matthew 26:38). The believer at the end of his strength prays to one who has felt that weight.

What if this is where I am? Then you are in the company of this man, of Elijah and of the psalmists, and the God who put their words in his book is not ashamed of you. Say it to him as they did. And do not stay there alone: tell a pastor or a trusted friend, and where despair has settled into depression, seek out a biblical counsellor, who will also ask you to have a medical check-up. Receive any treatment the doctor recommends without shame, as you would for any other illness; taking medicine is no failure of faith. If you are thinking of ending your life, tell someone today, and if you are in danger now, call the emergency services at once.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–24 — But This I Call to Mind
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hope returns to the man in the ruins, not because anything around him has changed, but because he deliberately calls to mind who the LORD is. Remembering his affliction only bows him down further (vv. 19–20). Then he calls something else to mind: the steadfast love of the LORD that never ceases, mercies that never run out and arrive fresh each morning, and a faithfulness great enough to be praised among the ashes (vv. 21–23). The land, the temple and the city are gone, but his true inheritance has not been touched: “The LORD is my portion”, so he will hope in him (v. 24). This is the centre of the book.
verseByVerse.theology: Hope in the ruins does not come from the circumstances but from calling to mind the unchanging character of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember my affliction and my wanderings, the wormwood and the gall! My soul continually remembers it and is bowed down within me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remembering his suffering only drives him lower, for brooding bends the soul double. He asks God to remember it, but his own memory of it is sinking him.

Remember my affliction. He calls on God to remember, the prayer the whole book prays. “My wanderings” is the homelessness of exile, and “the wormwood and the gall” are the bitterness again, gall being a byword for poison.

My soul continually remembers it. He cannot stop thinking about it, and the more he thinks, the lower he sinks. Brooding turns the same pain over and over until the soul is bowed down.

The wormwood and the gall. At Golgotha “they offered him wine to drink, mixed with gall”, and Jesus would not drink it (Matthew 27:34). He had come to drink another cup, the bitterness of God’s wrath, to the bottom.

In everyday life. Many people live exactly here, replaying the betrayal, the diagnosis, the mistake or the loss night after night. The next verse does not tell him to stop remembering. It tells him what else to remember.

verseByVerse.quote: But this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope: The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nothing around him has changed, but he deliberately calls to mind the LORD’s unfailing steadfast love, his inexhaustible mercies and his great faithfulness, and hope comes back. This is the hinge of the whole book.

But this I call to mind. The city is still in ruins, his body still broken, the enemies still laughing. What has changed is what he brings to mind. He makes himself remember, the way you take hold of a railing in the dark.

How hope works. In Scripture hope is not a mood that comes over you; it grows from telling yourself the truth. David did it when his men spoke of stoning him: “David strengthened himself in the LORD his God” (1 Samuel 30:6). A psalmist did it: “I will remember the deeds of the LORD; yes, I will remember your wonders of old” (Psalm 77:11). You may not be able to feel your way out of despair, but you can call something to mind, and for the believer the Holy Spirit does the reminding: he will “bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you” (John 14:26). What this man calls to mind is not a technique but a fact about God.

The steadfast love of the LORD. Steadfast love is God’s loyal, committed love to his covenant people, the love he proclaimed to Moses: “a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). It has bound itself by promise and will not let go. John says that in Jesus this God came to live among us, “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14, 17), and at the cross that love was shown beyond all doubt (Romans 5:8).

His mercies never come to an end. In chapter 2 the Lord swallowed up “without mercy” (2:2). The mercy had been withheld from the city’s walls; it had not been exhausted in God’s heart.

New every morning. Like the manna in the wilderness: “Morning by morning they gathered it, each as much as he could eat” (Exodus 16:21). It could not be stored; each day needed that day’s gift. Yesterday’s mercy was enough for yesterday; today’s is waiting for today, and tomorrow’s will be there tomorrow. That is why Jesus taught us to pray, “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matthew 6:11), and not to be anxious about tomorrow (Matthew 6:34).

Great is your faithfulness. Now he turns and speaks straight to God. Not ‘great was your faithfulness’ in the good old days, but great is, now, among the ashes. God’s faithfulness is measured not by our circumstances but by his promises, and he keeps them: “If we are faithless, he remains faithful” (2 Timothy 2:13).

In everyday life. Some mornings the weight comes back before you have even opened your eyes. On those mornings, remember that there is a fresh supply of mercy which did not exist last night, made for this morning.

The fresh start we cannot give ourselves. Our culture loves new beginnings: the gyms fill up in January, and apps promise a new you in thirty days. The instinct is sound, for we know we need mornings. But the modern fresh start has to be manufactured by the very person who needs it, which is why it so often runs out by February. The moralist says try harder, the self-help book says believe in yourself, and both lay the weight on the one who is exhausted. Lamentations offers a different morning. The newness is not in the man but in God’s mercy, which is there before he wakes and does not depend on how yesterday went. The gift comes first, and change grows out of it. Very early on the first day of the week, some women went to a tomb to anoint a body, and found that God had begun something new before they arrived (Mark 16:2–6). That is the shape of every Christian morning: mercy is up before we are.

Textual note. In verse 22 the ESV follows the Syriac and the Targum (ancient Syriac and Aramaic versions). The Hebrew text reads ‘Because of the steadfast love of the LORD, we are not cut off’, which the King James Version gives as ‘It is of the LORD’s mercies that we are not consumed’. Both readings stand on the same truth: either God’s love never ceases, or it is the reason we have not ceased. Jerusalem had been struck to the ground but not wiped out; there were survivors, and someone was left alive to write this poem, proof that God’s love had not run out.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV follows the Syriac and Targum in v. 22 (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: "The LORD is my portion," says my soul, "therefore I will hope in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the land and everything else are lost, the LORD himself remains his portion, so he resolves to hope in him.

The LORD is my portion. A portion was a share of the inheritance, land to live on and farm. When Israel entered Canaan, every tribe received a portion except Levi, and to Aaron the priest God said, “You shall have no inheritance in their land… I am your portion and your inheritance” (Numbers 18:20). Now every Israelite stands where the priests stood. The land is lost, “Our inheritance has been turned over to strangers” (5:2), and the house, the fields and the temple are gone. Yet the man says he still has his portion: the LORD himself.

Where hope becomes unshakeable. If your portion is your health, your family, your reputation or your savings, it can be taken, and your hope goes with it. If your portion is the LORD, nothing can take it: “My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever” (Psalm 73:26).

Therefore I will hope in him. He is talking to himself again, as in verse 21. Not ‘I feel hopeful’ but “I will hope”: hope is a decision made on the ground of who God is.

Not only himself but his Son. Christians can say this with more certainty still, because God has given us not only himself but his Son: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–39 — It Is Good to Wait Quietly
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Having found the LORD good, the man teaches what he has learned about suffering under God’s hand. The one who had forgotten what good is now says “good” three times: the LORD is good to those who wait for him, it is good to wait quietly, and good to bear the yoke while young (vv. 25–27). So the sufferer sits in humble silence with his mouth in the dust and does not hit back (vv. 28–30), because the Lord will not cast off forever and does not afflict from his heart (vv. 31–33). He never approves of injustice (vv. 34–36), yet nothing happens unless he has commanded it, so a living man should not complain but turn (vv. 37–39).
verseByVerse.theology: God rules over affliction and is never cruel in it, and he never approves of the injustice he turns to his own purposes.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is good to those who wait for him, to the soul who seeks him. It is good that one should wait quietly for the salvation of the LORD. It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD is good to those who wait for him, so it is good to wait quietly for his salvation, and good to learn under his yoke while young. The good he could not find in his circumstances (v. 17) he has found in God.

The LORD is good. He had forgotten what good is; now the word comes back three times, and in Hebrew each of these three verses begins with it.

To those who wait for him. Waiting in the Bible is not passive. It is leaning your whole weight on God while nothing seems to happen, and it is paired with “the soul who seeks him”: “they who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength” (Isaiah 40:31).

Wait quietly. Not without prayer, for this book is full of loud prayer, but without the fretting panic that tries to force God’s hand or find a way out apart from him. “In quietness and in trust shall be your strength” (Isaiah 30:15); “Be still before the LORD and wait patiently for him” (Psalm 37:7).

Bear the yoke in his youth. A young ox learns to pull by wearing the yoke. It chafes, but an animal that never bore a yoke is useless for the plough. Hard things learned early shape a life: “Before I was afflicted I went astray, but now I keep your word” (Psalm 119:67).

The waiting is not empty. The LORD has already kept his greatest promise: “when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son” (Galatians 4:4). A God who kept that word will keep the rest, and Christ “will appear a second time” to save “those who are eagerly waiting for him” (Hebrews 9:28). And there is one yoke every young person should take up as early as possible: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29).

How do I wait for the LORD? Waiting is what you do when the scan results are not back, the job has not come, the wandering child has not phoned. Keep seeking. The verse pairs waiting with seeking, so keep reading and praying even when it feels dry. Refuse the shortcut. Name the panicked move you are tempted to make, the angry message or the dishonest fix, and decline it. Do the next ordinary thing. Waiting is not idleness: cook the meal, go to work, answer the letter. Rehearse what he has done, as the poet did in verses 21–24.

Should the young be spared every hardship? Many loving parents now think so, and the instinct comes from a good place. But Greg Lukianoff and Jonathan Haidt argued in The Coddling of the American Mind (2018) that a well-meant culture of protection has taught many young people a falsehood: that what does not kill you makes you weaker. People, they suggested, are less like fine china than like the immune system, which grows strong by meeting challenges, not by being sealed off from them. Lamentations knew it long ago: some yokes are gifts. Yet the Bible is just as wary of the opposite answer, the voice that says toughen up and rely on yourself, for grit can produce a hard person as easily as a good one. What the young need is neither bubble wrap nor a drill sergeant but a Father. A yoke can be borne, even welcomed, when you know whose hand has laid it on you and that he means it for your good. The Son himself “learned obedience through what he suffered” (Hebrews 5:8), and because he walked that road first, no young believer carries a yoke alone.

verseByVerse.quote: Let him sit alone in silence when it is laid on him; let him put his mouth in the dust— there may yet be hope; let him give his cheek to the one who strikes, and let him be filled with insults.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God lays affliction on him, the sufferer should bow in humble silence and not hit back, for there may yet be hope.

Let him sit alone in silence. The first response to the yoke is not to argue with it or explain it. There is a silence of rebellion, sulking at God; this is the other kind, the silence of someone who has recognised God’s hand: “I am mute; I do not open my mouth, for it is you who have done it” (Psalm 39:9).

There may yet be hope. To put your mouth in the dust is to lie face down, as a subject before a king. And a quiet line is tucked in: “there may yet be hope”. Not a guarantee of how things will turn out, but a door left open. Humility is where hope can begin, because it stops demanding and starts trusting: “Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you” (1 Peter 5:6).

Let him give his cheek to the one who strikes. A man who has stopped fighting God no longer needs to hit back at those God uses to humble him.

Jesus gave his cheek because we had sinned. The Servant of the LORD said, “I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard” (Isaiah 50:6). At his trial, “they spit in his face and struck him” (Matthew 26:67), and “When he was reviled, he did not revile in return… but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23). The man in Lamentations gave his cheek because he had sinned; Jesus gave his because we had.

What it does not mean. The chapter is about accepting God’s discipline humbly, not about excusing human cruelty; a few verses later it says plainly that the Lord does not approve of injustice (vv. 34–36). This verse does not tell anyone to stay in harm’s way or to treat abuse as God’s will: anyone being abused should seek safety at once, and the abuse should be reported.

verseByVerse.quote: For the Lord will not cast off forever, for, though he cause grief, he will have compassion according to the abundance of his steadfast love; for he does not afflict from his heart or grieve the children of men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s affliction of his people is never final, it is always followed by abundant compassion, and it does not come from his heart. Here are three reasons for hope, each beginning “for”.

The Lord will not cast off forever. Discipline has an end, even when you cannot see it: “For his anger is but for a moment, and his favor is for a lifetime. Weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning” (Psalm 30:5).

He will have compassion. The grief is real (“though he cause grief”), but compassion follows it, measured “according to the abundance of his steadfast love”. The grief has a limit; the love does not.

He does not afflict from his heart. God does afflict, and this book has not hidden it for a moment. But it is not what he delights in, nor the centre of who he is. Ezekiel heard God say, “I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live” (Ezekiel 33:11), and Isaiah called judgment God’s “strange” deed and “alien” work (Isaiah 28:21). Mercy is his heart; judgment is the work his holiness requires when mercy is refused.

The proof at the cross. What is in God’s heart is shown at the cross, where he gave his Son out of love, so that his just anger against sin would be fully borne and his compassion could flow freely to sinners.

When God disciplines his children. He is not enjoying it: “he disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness” (Hebrews 12:10). A father who must correct his child does it with a heavy heart, and God’s heart is heavier and kinder than any father’s.

verseByVerse.quote: To crush underfoot all the prisoners of the earth, to deny a man justice in the presence of the Most High, to subvert a man in his lawsuit, the Lord does not approve.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord sees every act of cruelty and injustice, even those done by the people he uses to judge, and he approves of none of them.

The Lord does not approve. The three verses build to one statement at the very end. Crushing prisoners, twisting justice in court, cheating someone in a lawsuit: God sees them all and approves of none.

In the presence of the Most High. Every courtroom on earth sits in the presence of a higher court. Injustice that no human judge corrects is not unseen. For anyone who has been wronged and never had justice, that is solid comfort; for anyone who has done the wronging, it is a solemn warning.

Why is this here? A person who has just said that his suffering comes from God’s hand may be tempted to think that everything done to him must therefore be right. It is not. The Babylonians who crushed Judah’s prisoners were God’s instrument, and they were also guilty. God’s rule over all things does not make him the author of anyone’s cruelty.

God meant it for good. Joseph could say to his brothers, “you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20), and both halves were true. At the cross the same double truth reached its peak: Jesus was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God”, and his killers were still “lawless men” (Acts 2:23).

verseByVerse.quote: Who has spoken and it came to pass, unless the Lord has commanded it? Is it not from the mouth of the Most High that good and bad come? Why should a living man complain, a man, about the punishment of his sins?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nothing happens unless the Lord has commanded it, good and bad alike, so a living man punished for his sins has no ground to complain against God.

Unless the Lord has commanded it? Now the other side of the truth. God disapproves of injustice, and yet nothing happens outside his command: human plans, Babylon’s included, come to pass only as God has ordained and directs them.

Good and bad. Job said, “Shall we receive good from God, and shall we not receive evil?” (Job 2:10), and God said through Isaiah, “I make well-being and create calamity” (Isaiah 45:7). The Bible holds this without apology, because the alternative is far worse: if there is disaster God does not control, then there is disaster with no purpose and no end.

Not a cold doctrine. It is what makes verse 22 possible. If God rules over the bad, his steadfast love can reach into it, limit it and use it: “for those who love God all things work together for good” (Romans 8:28).

Why should a living man complain? After everything, he is still breathing, which the Hebrew reading of verse 22 counts a mercy; the punishment has been less than the sin. To complain here is not to lament but to grumble that God is unfair. Lament says, ‘Lord, this hurts; please look.’ Complaint says, ‘Lord, I don’t deserve this.’ The man has already admitted that he bears “the punishment of his sins”, so he may lament, and he must not complain.

What Christians receive instead. We may bring every tear to God. But no Christian ever receives what his sins deserve, because Christ received it: “He does not deal with us according to our sins, nor repay us according to our iniquities” (Psalm 103:10).

Does this mean my own suffering is punishment for my sin? These words speak of Judah’s judgment, announced long before (Deuteronomy 28; 2:17). Not all suffering is punishment for a particular sin: Job was blameless, and Jesus said of the man born blind, “It was not that this man sinned” (John 9:3). For a believer, Christ bore the punishment of sin (Isaiah 53:5); hardship may be a Father’s discipline (Hebrews 12:6), but it is never his condemnation (Romans 8:1). Where we have sinned, the right response is the next verse: “Let us test and examine our ways, and return to the LORD!”

Where Christians differ: does God ordain calamity, or only permit it? Many Christians, Arminians among them, hold that God permits disasters and sinful acts but does not ordain them, so that verse 37 means nothing happens without his allowing it; open theists go further and say he cannot know or prevent much of it. This commentary’s view: “commanded” and “from the mouth of the Most High” (vv. 37–38) say more than permission. God ordains whatever comes to pass, the fall of Jerusalem included, yet he is not the author of sin, he does not afflict from his heart (v. 33), and he approves of no injustice (vv. 34–36). That is why the sufferer can bring his grief to God, and why his hope does not hang on chance.

Uncertain wording. The end of verse 39 is compressed in Hebrew, literally ‘a man, over his sins’, and the word for sin can also mean its penalty, which is how the ESV takes it (“the punishment of his sins”). Most translations read the line as part of the question; some take it as the answer: instead of complaining about his lot, let each man grieve over his own sins. Either way it leads straight into verse 40.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 40–54 — Let Us Test and Examine Our Ways
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Suffering rightly received turns into repentance, and repentance keeps praying until God looks down. The “I” of the chapter becomes “we”: let us test our ways and return to the LORD, lifting up hearts as well as hands (vv. 40–41). The confession is short and honest, and so is the complaint: God has not yet forgiven, and has wrapped himself in anger and in a cloud that no prayer can pass (vv. 42–45). Enemies jeer, disaster piles on disaster, and the speaker’s tears run like rivers for his people (vv. 46–48). He will not stop weeping until the LORD looks down from heaven (vv. 49–51), and he remembers the pit where the water closed over his head and he said, “I am lost” (vv. 52–54).
verseByVerse.theology: Real repentance examines its own ways, confesses without excuse, and keeps praying until God looks down.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us test and examine our ways, and return to the LORD! Let us lift up our hearts and hands to God in heaven: "We have transgressed and rebelled, and you have not forgiven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The right response to God’s hand is to examine our own ways and come back to him with our hearts, confessing our sin without excuse even while its consequences remain. Here the “I” of the chapter becomes “us”.

Let us test and examine our ways. Not God’s ways but ours. That is backwards from how most people react: we ask why God allowed this; Lamentations asks what we have done and where we need to turn. It is the prodigal son in the far country: “when he came to himself”, he said, “I will arise and go to my father” (Luke 15:17–18).

And return to the LORD! Examination is not an end in itself. Self-examination that stays turned inward becomes morbid; self-examination that leads to God becomes repentance: “Search me, O God, and know my heart!… And see if there be any grievous way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting!” (Psalm 139:23–24).

Let us lift up our hearts and hands. Lifting hands was the posture of prayer, and Judah had lifted plenty of hands in the temple. What was missing was the heart: “rend your hearts and not your garments” (Joel 2:13). God wants the inside to go up with the outside.

And you have not forgiven. The confession is short and makes no excuses. Then comes an honest, painful line: they have confessed, and the exile goes on. Confessing a sin does not always remove its consequences in this life, even for Christians.

The guilt does not linger. But the Christian can say what the exiles could not yet say, because Christ has come: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9). The consequences may linger; the guilt does not, because Christ’s perfect obedience and death are counted as ours: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). And the same Spirit who brings us back gives power to walk in new ways (Romans 8:4).

How do I examine my ways? Self-examination can slide into endless brooding, so keep it simple and short. Ask him first. Pray Psalm 139 and ask God to show you, rather than digging alone. Look at the week, not your whole life: words spoken, money spent, people avoided, what you worried about most. Name one thing plainly, the sharp email or the small lie that made the evening easier, without excuses. Turn it into a step. Returning means doing something: an apology, a repayment, a habit dropped. And do it all looking at Christ more than at yourself, as someone already welcomed. The son in the far country rehearsed his speech, but “while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him” (Luke 15:20).

verseByVerse.quote: "You have wrapped yourself with anger and pursued us, killing without pity; you have wrapped yourself with a cloud so that no prayer can pass through. You have made us scum and garbage among the peoples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people confess that God has pursued them in anger and hidden himself behind a cloud that blocks their prayers, leaving them the refuse of the nations.

You have wrapped yourself. Twice: first with anger, then with a cloud. The cloud that once filled the temple with glory now blocks prayer like a wall: “your iniquities have made a separation between you and your God, and your sins have hidden his face from you so that he does not hear” (Isaiah 59:2).

Scum and garbage among the peoples. The chosen people have become the rubbish of the nations, what everyone else throws away.

No cloud that prayer cannot pass through. When Jesus died, “the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom” (Matthew 27:51): the barrier between sinners and God was opened from God’s side. Christ has entered “into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf” (Hebrews 9:24), and “he always lives to make intercession” for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). For anyone in Christ, there is no cloud that prayer cannot pass through.

The refuse of all things. Paul used almost the same words for an apostle’s life: “We have become, and are still, like the scum of the world, the refuse of all things” (1 Corinthians 4:13). For him it was not judgment but the privilege of following a Lord who was himself treated as refuse, crucified outside the city like something thrown out. What Judah suffered as the penalty of sin, Christ took on as the price of love, and his people share it as the mark of belonging to him.

verseByVerse.quote: "All our enemies open their mouths against us; panic and pitfall have come upon us, devastation and destruction; my eyes flow with rivers of tears because of the destruction of the daughter of my people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Surrounded by jeering enemies and piled-up disaster, the speaker weeps rivers of tears, now not for himself but for his people.

Panic and pitfall. The calamity comes in pairs that pile on each other, “panic and pitfall”, “devastation and destruction”: terror inside, traps outside, ruin all round. In Hebrew the first pair sound alike, as the English tries to show; Isaiah used the same sound-play: “Terror and the pit and the snare” (Isaiah 24:17).

My eyes flow with rivers of tears. Personal pain has become grief for “the daughter of my people”. Pain can shrink us until we see nothing but ourselves, or enlarge us so that we weep with those who weep (Romans 12:15). Jesus, riding into the city where he would die, wept over it (Luke 19:41).

verseByVerse.quote: "My eyes will flow without ceasing, without respite, until the LORD from heaven looks down and sees; my eyes cause me grief at the fate of all the daughters of my city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He will keep weeping and praying until the LORD looks down from heaven, his heart broken by what he has seen happen to the women of his city.

Until the LORD from heaven looks down. He will not stop until God looks. Isaiah prayed the same: “Look down from heaven and see, from your holy and beautiful habitation” (Isaiah 63:15). Jesus told a parable “to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart” (Luke 18:1). Some prayers need to be prayed many times, for many years, until the Lord looks down. Do not stop praying them.

All the daughters of my city. He has watched the young women of Jerusalem suffer (1:4, 18; 2:21), and their faces do not leave him. Grief for others is not weakness; it is a heart like God’s.

Uncertain wording. “My eyes cause me grief” is an unusual expression in Hebrew, literally something like ‘my eye deals harshly with my soul’. It may mean that what he has seen torments him, or that his endless weeping is wearing his life away. Either way, his grief for others has become his own wound.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have been hunted like a bird by those who were my enemies without cause; they flung me alive into the pit and cast stones on me; water closed over my head; I said, 'I am lost.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hated without cause, he was thrown alive into a pit, the water closed over his head, and he thought it was the end.

Hunted like a bird. His enemies hunted him “without cause”: he had done them no wrong. The phrase echoes through the psalms (“without cause they dug a pit for my life”, Psalm 35:7), and Jesus took it up for himself: “They hated me without a cause” (John 15:25). The righteous sufferer hated for no reason is found most completely in Christ.

They flung me alive into the pit. Thrown into a pit alive, with stones thrown down on top. It is hard not to think of Jeremiah, whose enemies “cast him into the cistern”, where “there was no water in the cistern, but only mud, and Jeremiah sank in the mud” (Jeremiah 38:6), expecting him to “die there of hunger” (Jeremiah 38:9). A cistern was a pit cut in the rock to store rainwater; dry or muddy, it made a ready prison.

Water closed over my head. Jonah said something very like it: “The waters closed in over me to take my life” (Jonah 2:5).

I said, ‘I am lost.’ Many believers have been here, at the moment when you say, ‘This is the end; there is no way out.’ The next verse shows that it is not where the story ends.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that “they flung me alive into the pit” may be rendered ‘they end my life in the pit’, for the Hebrew verb can mean to put an end to. Either way, they meant him to die there.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 55–66 — You Came Near When I Called
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The God who seemed to shut out prayer comes near when he is called, and the chapter ends with a man who has handed his whole case to him. From the depths of the pit the man called; the LORD heard, came near and said, “Do not fear!” (vv. 55–57). He took up the man’s cause and redeemed his life, and he has seen every wrong done to him and heard every taunt and plot (vv. 58–63). So the man leaves his enemies with God, asking him to repay them according to their deeds (vv. 64–66). Nothing outside has changed yet, but he has met God in the pit, and that is enough to wait on.
verseByVerse.theology: The God who seemed to shut out prayer is the God who comes near, speaks peace and redeems.

verseByVerse.quote: "I called on your name, O LORD, from the depths of the pit; you heard my plea, 'Do not close your ear to my cry for help!' You came near when I called on you; you said, 'Do not fear!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
From the bottom of the pit he called on the LORD, and the God who had seemed to shut out his prayer heard him, came near and said, “Do not fear!”

From the depths of the pit. No one can fall so far that he is out of calling distance: “Out of the depths I cry to you, O LORD!” (Psalm 130:1).

You heard my plea. Earlier he said, “he shuts out my prayer” (v. 8), and the people said, “no prayer can pass through” (v. 44). Now: “you heard my plea”. What felt like a locked door was not locked forever. For anyone praying through the silence, how it feels now is not the last word on whether God hears.

You said, ‘Do not fear!’ God, who had seemed like a bear, a lion and an archer, comes near and says only, “Do not fear!” It is the word he speaks again and again to his frightened people, “fear not, for I am with you” (Isaiah 41:10), and the word Jesus spoke on the stormy lake: “Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid” (Matthew 14:27).

He went down into the pit. The risen Christ said to John, who fell at his feet as though dead, “Fear not, I am the first and the last, and the living one. I died, and behold I am alive forevermore” (Revelation 1:17–18). The God who came near to the man in the pit came near to us in person, went down into the pit of death himself, and came back up.

verseByVerse.quote: "You have taken up my cause, O Lord; you have redeemed my life. You have seen the wrong done to me, O LORD; judge my cause. You have seen all their vengeance, all their plots against me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD has taken up his case like an advocate and paid to set him free, and he has seen every wrong done to him, so the man leaves the verdict with him.

You have taken up my cause. Two legal pictures. God has become his advocate in court, and he has “redeemed my life”, paying to set him free as a relative bought back a family member sold into slavery. Jeremiah had promised exactly this for the exiles: “Their Redeemer is strong; the LORD of hosts is his name. He will surely plead their cause” (Jeremiah 50:34).

You have seen the wrong done to me. The prayer of chapter 1 was “Look, O LORD, and see” (1:11). Now he knows God has seen; nothing done in secret against God’s people is hidden from him. So he asks God to “judge my cause”, handing his case to the one Judge who sees everything instead of taking justice into his own hands.

Christ our advocate. “If anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 John 2:1). Our advocate does not only plead our case; he paid our debt. He is both the lawyer and the ransom.

verseByVerse.quote: "You have heard their taunts, O LORD, all their plots against me. The lips and thoughts of my assailants are against me all the day long. Behold their sitting and their rising; I am the object of their taunts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD has heard every taunt and knows every plot of the man’s enemies, from morning to night.

You have heard their taunts. God has seen the wrong (vv. 59–60), and he has heard it too: he knows the enemies’ “lips and thoughts”.

Their sitting and their rising. Everything they do from morning to night: whether they sit down or get up, they are mocking him. “You know when I sit down and when I rise up” (Psalm 139:2): the God who knows every movement of his own people knows every movement of their enemies.

In everyday life. If you are being slandered, mocked or plotted against, this is where to take it: not into a counter-campaign, but to the God who has seen and heard and knows.

verseByVerse.quote: "You will repay them, O LORD, according to the work of their hands. You will give them dullness of heart; your curse will be on them. You will pursue them in anger and destroy them from under your heavens, O LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He leaves his enemies with God, asking him to repay them with justice, as he has repaid his own people.

You will repay them. The man is either declaring what God will do or asking him to do it (see the box below). Either way he is leaving it with God.

According to the work of their hands. What he asks is simply justice, not more than they deserve. The Bible never tells believers to pretend that evil does not matter; God himself “considers it just to repay with affliction those who afflict you” (2 Thessalonians 1:6).

Dullness of heart. A heart that can no longer take in the truth, the judgment God pronounced through Isaiah on a people who would not listen: “Make the heart of this people dull, and their ears heavy, and blind their eyes” (Isaiah 6:10). There is something more fearful than pain: a heart that no longer hears God. It is also a reason to pray, while hearts can still hear, for those who have not yet turned.

You will pursue them in anger. The people had said to God, “You have wrapped yourself with anger and pursued us” (v. 43). The prayer asks God to do to Babylon what he has done to Judah, as Zion had asked in the first poem (1:22). God’s justice has no favourites: if his own people did not escape it, their oppressors will not either.

From under your heavens. These are the chapter’s last words, and the ESV notes that the Hebrew reads ‘the heavens of the LORD’. The chapter that began in darkness ends looking up at the LORD’s heavens, from which the man had waited for the LORD to look down (v. 50). He has not yet seen the end, but he has seen God come near, and that is enough to wait on.

Vengeance in God’s hands. See where the vengeance is placed: in God’s hands, not the man’s. That is the New Testament command: “never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God” (Romans 12:19). A believer who has truly handed justice over to God is free from bitterness, free to forgive, even free to pray for his enemies, as Jesus did on the cross (Luke 23:34). For the enemy who repents, Christ has already borne the curse (Galatians 3:13).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew verbs of verses 64–66 can be read either as statements or as prayers, and the ESV notes the alternatives: ‘Repay them’, ‘Give them’, ‘Pursue them’, and ‘place your curse’ for “your curse will be on them”. The word translated “dullness” occurs only here; it seems to mean a covering over the heart, and older translations rendered it ‘sorrow of heart’. Either way it describes a heart closed by judgment.

3.title: His Mercies Are New Every Morning
3.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 3 is the centre of the book and its highest point. After two poems about the ruined city, a single man speaks out of the same disaster, in a poem that gives three verses to each letter of the Hebrew alphabet (see the introduction).

The message. When everything is lost and God himself seems to be the enemy, hope is found not in a change of circumstances but in calling to mind who the LORD is. His steadfast love never ceases, his mercies are new every morning, and he remains the portion of his people when everything else is gone. He rules even over disaster, yet does not afflict from his heart, and he comes near to those who call to him from the pit.

Why it was said. The survivors of Jerusalem’s fall had lost city, temple, king and land, and many felt that God had shut out their prayers for good (see the introduction). They needed to know whether any hope was left, and how to suffer under God’s hand without denying their sin or despairing of his mercy.

How the chapter makes its case. The man tells the whole truth about his pain, speaking of God as his attacker until his hope is gone (vv. 1–18). Then comes the turn, “But this I call to mind”: the LORD’s steadfast love and faithfulness, and the LORD himself as his portion (vv. 19–24). From there he teaches what he has learned: wait quietly under the yoke, for the Lord will not cast off forever, does not approve of injustice, and rules over good and bad alike (vv. 25–39). Then the people examine their ways, confess and weep until God looks down (vv. 40–54). Finally he remembers how the LORD heard him from the pit and said, “Do not fear!”, and he leaves his enemies to God’s justice (vv. 55–66).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by the character of God revealed in him. The man who is mocked, given gall, struck on the cheek, hated without cause and thrown into the pit is a pattern of the one who suffered all of it with no sin of his own. The steadfast love the man calls to mind came to live among us in Jesus, “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14), and God showed what is truly in his heart by giving his Son. Because Christ went down into the pit of death and rose again, no believer calls from the depths unheard.

For us. When the weight comes back before you have opened your eyes, tell God the truth about your pain, then deliberately call to mind who he is. In Christ his mercies are new this morning, and he is a portion that no loss can take away.
3.theology:
A believer may say his hope is gone and still be speaking to the LORD (v. 18); hope returns by calling to mind the character of God (v. 21). The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases, and his mercies are new every morning; his faithfulness is great even among the ashes (vv. 22-23; Exod 34:6; 2 Tim 2:13). When every earthly portion is lost, the LORD himself remains the portion of his people (v. 24; Num 18:20; Ps 73:26).

Affliction is sent by God, yet it does not come from his heart; for his people, grief is always followed by compassion as great as his steadfast love (vv. 31-33; Ezek 33:11; Heb 12:10).

God rules over good and bad alike, yet he never approves of human injustice; the instruments of his judgment remain guilty (vv. 34-38; Gen 50:20; Acts 2:23).

Lament is right; complaint against God's justice is not (v. 39). True repentance examines its own ways and confesses without excuse (vv. 40-42).

God hears prayer from the depths, comes near, and says Do not fear; he is his people's advocate and redeemer (vv. 55-58; Jer 50:34). In Christ the barrier to prayer is torn away, and the believer has an advocate who also paid the ransom (Matt 27:51; Heb 7:25; 1 John 2:1).

Justice against enemies belongs to God, and leaving it with him sets the believer free to forgive (vv. 64-66; Rom 12:19; Luke 23:34).

The man of affliction points beyond himself to Christ, who suffered not for his own sins but for ours (vv. 14, 30, 52-53; Isa 50:6; John 15:25; 1 Pet 2:23).
3.examples:
The chapter begins in darkness without any light, with prayers that seem to hit the ceiling, bread full of gravel, and a man who has forgotten what good is and replays the same pain night after night.

Then comes the turn: But this I call to mind, like taking hold of a railing in the dark. Mercy is gathered like manna, morning by morning, and cannot be stored up; the land is lost, and the LORD turns out to be the portion no one can take away. A young ox learns to pull, a mouth in the dust finds a door left open, and a Father corrects with a heavy heart.

At the end a man at the bottom of a cistern calls, and the God who tore the curtain from top to bottom comes near and says, Do not fear!

keyVerse.quote: The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness.
keyVerse.note: These verses are the hinge of the chapter and of the whole book. Nothing around the poet had changed, yet calling to mind the LORD’s covenant love and faithfulness turned despair into hope (v. 21). In Christ that steadfast love has come in person, and his mercies meet his people fresh every morning.

3.reflection:
The man in verses 1–18 speaks to God with startling honesty, even calling him a bear and an archer. Why do you think Scripture includes prayers like this, and what would change if you prayed more honestly?

Nothing in the poet’s circumstances changed between verse 18 and verse 21; what changed was what he called to mind. Which truths about God do you most need to call to mind on hard mornings, and how could you make a habit of it?

Verses 31–39 say both that the Lord rules over good and bad and that he does not afflict from his heart or approve of injustice. How do these truths together help a suffering believer? Where might holding only one of them lead us astray?

The chapter moves from “I” to “we”, and from weeping for oneself to weeping for others (vv. 40–51). How can suffering make us more or less able to care for others, and whom could you pray for or weep with this week?
