verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sin had stripped Jerusalem of the dignity and tenderness God gave it, and the poem makes us look. Gold has grown dim and holy stones lie in the street, for the precious sons of Zion, worth their weight in gold, are treated like cheap clay pots (vv. 1–2). Starving children beg and no one has anything to give, while the rich cling to ash heaps (vv. 3–5). The punishment is heavier than Sodom’s, which fell in a moment, and the once-radiant princes are shrivelled beyond recognition (vv. 6–8). Those killed by the sword were better off than those who starved, and at the very bottom, loving mothers ate their own children, as Moses had warned (vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.theology: Sin does not only bring punishment; it strips a people of the dignity and tenderness God gave them.

verseByVerse.quote: How the gold has grown dim, how the pure gold is changed! The holy stones lie scattered at the head of every street. The precious sons of Zion, worth their weight in fine gold, how they are regarded as earthen pots, the work of a potter's hands!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people of Zion, precious as gold to God, have been treated as worthless and broken like cheap clay pots. The poet is mourning not the temple treasury but people.

How the gold has grown dim. The poem opens with the same cry as chapters 1 and 2, “How”, and a picture of treasure ruined. Pure gold does not tarnish, yet this gold has grown dim, and holy stones lie in the gutters.

Regarded as earthen pots. Earthen pots were the cheapest things in a household, used, cracked and thrown on the rubbish heap. The young men of Jerusalem, precious as gold, are treated as disposable: Babylon killed them, starved them and marched them off as if they had no value at all. The picture is Jeremiah’s own: he was sent to smash a potter’s flask before the city’s leaders as a sign of what God would do to it (Jeremiah 19:10–11).

Where worth comes from. A person’s worth does not come from how others treat him. God said to his people, “you are precious in my eyes, and honored, and I love you” (Isaiah 43:4), and their value did not change when Babylon despised them.

Treasure in jars of clay. Paul takes up the clay pot and turns it to glory: “we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us” (2 Corinthians 4:7). The world may regard God’s people as earthen pots, but he has filled them with treasure and paid for them, “not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19).

verseByVerse.quote: Even jackals offer the breast; they nurse their young; but the daughter of my people has become cruel, like the ostriches in the wilderness. The tongue of the nursing infant sticks to the roof of its mouth for thirst; the children beg for food, but no one gives to them. Those who once feasted on delicacies perish in the streets; those who were brought up in purple embrace ash heaps.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The famine has done worse than kill: it has hardened mothers’ hearts, left children begging with no one able to feed them, and brought the wealthy down to the rubbish heaps.

Even jackals offer the breast. Jackals were despised scavengers, yet even they feed their young. In the book of Job the ostrich is the careless mother: “she leaves her eggs to the earth… She deals cruelly with her young, as if they were not hers” (Job 39:14, 16).

The daughter of my people has become cruel. Mothers who would have given their lives for their children can no longer feed them, and in the desperation of hunger some stop trying. This is the second time Lamentations makes us look at hungry children (2:11–12), and it will not let us look away. Sin’s consequences reach down into the most natural affections God created.

The children beg for food. “No one gives to them”, not because no one loves them, but because no one has anything left. Purple was the colour of royalty and wealth, and children raised in the best homes of Jerusalem now cling to rubbish heaps, looking for anything to eat.

A rich man clothed in purple. Jesus told of a rich man “clothed in purple” who feasted every day while a beggar lay at his gate, and of the reversal that came: “you in your lifetime received your good things, and Lazarus in like manner bad things; but now he is comforted here, and you are in anguish” (Luke 16:19, 25). Wealth is no protection on the day God overturns things; the only safe way to be rich is to be rich toward God (Luke 12:21).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew for “jackals” is spelled almost like the word for a great sea creature, so older translations read ‘sea monsters’. Most now take it as jackals, wild creatures like the ostrich beside them. Either way, even wild animals feed their young.

verseByVerse.quote: For the chastisement of the daughter of my people has been greater than the punishment of Sodom, which was overthrown in a moment, and no hands were wrung for her. Her princes were purer than snow, whiter than milk; their bodies were more ruddy than coral, the beauty of their form was like sapphire. Now their face is blacker than soot; they are not recognized in the streets; their skin has shriveled on their bones; it has become as dry as wood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem’s punishment has been heavier than Sodom’s, and her once-radiant princes are shrivelled beyond recognition. On one reading of verse 6, her sin was greater than Sodom’s too.

Greater than the punishment of Sodom. Sodom was destroyed “in a moment”. Jerusalem’s agony went on and on through a long siege and a slow famine, and in that sense her suffering was greater.

A deeper reading. The ESV notes that “chastisement” can be rendered ‘iniquity’, and “punishment” ‘sin’. Then the verse says that Jerusalem’s iniquity was greater than Sodom’s sin, as Ezekiel said: “your sister Sodom and her daughters have not done as you and your daughters have done” (Ezekiel 16:48). How could that be? Because Jerusalem had received what Sodom never had: the law, the temple, the prophets, the covenant. “Everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required” (Luke 12:48). Jesus said the same to the towns where he had done his mighty works: “it will be more tolerable on the day of judgment for the land of Sodom than for you” (Matthew 11:24).

Her princes were purer than snow. The young nobles had been the picture of health and beauty. Now starvation has blackened their faces and shrunk their skin onto their bones, and their own neighbours do not recognise them.

Beauty that fades. Human beauty and strength are real gifts, and they are fragile: “man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7). And there was one whose “appearance was so marred, beyond human semblance” (Isaiah 52:14), not because of his sin but so that ours could be dealt with.

For those raised with the Bible. For anyone who has grown up with the Bible, privilege is no shelter from judgment; it makes us more answerable. Yet the same Jesus who warned those towns went on to say, “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden” (Matthew 11:28).

Uncertain wording. Besides the double meaning of “chastisement” and “punishment”, the ESV notes that the meaning of “no hands were wrung for her” (v. 6) is uncertain. It may mean that no one grieved for Sodom, or that no human hand was laid on her, because God overthrew her directly. The ESV also notes that the meaning of “the beauty of their form” (v. 7) is uncertain, and that the stone called “sapphire” is literally lapis lazuli, a deep blue stone.

verseByVerse.quote: Happier were the victims of the sword than the victims of hunger, who wasted away, pierced by lack of the fruits of the field. The hands of compassionate women have boiled their own children; they became their food during the destruction of the daughter of my people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Starvation was worse than the sword, and at the very bottom of the siege, loving mothers ate their own children. The Bible does not hide this, because we need to see where sin leads.

Happier were the victims of the sword. Death by the sword was quick; death by famine was slow, a wasting away, “pierced” not by a blade but by hunger. The poet counts those who died quickly the fortunate ones.

The hands of compassionate women. Not monsters but ordinary loving mothers were driven by starvation to eat their own children. Moses had warned of exactly this, in almost unbearable detail: the most tender woman among them would “eat them secretly, in the siege and in the distress with which your enemy shall distress you in your towns” (Deuteronomy 28:56–57). It had happened once before, in the siege of Samaria (2 Kings 6:28–29).

Not monsters. The word “compassionate” will not let the reader despise these women. Their tenderness is the measure of how terrible the siege was, and the poem grieves for them as well as for their children. The one who later longed over this same city as a hen gathers her brood under her wings (Matthew 23:37) is not without pity for mothers broken by its fall.

Why does God let such things be recorded? Because we need to know what sin really is, and where it leads when God finally gives a people over to it. A nation’s long rebellion, and the siege it brought, can unravel everything good he made, down to a mother’s love. Only when we see that clearly do we understand why the cross had to be so terrible, and why grace is so amazing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–16 — For the Sins of Her Prophets
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The fall of the city everyone thought could not fall was the LORD’s doing, and its root lay with the men who should have led the people to God. The LORD poured out his anger and burned Zion to its foundations, though no king on earth had believed an enemy could enter its gates (vv. 11–12). It happened for the sins of the prophets and priests who shed righteous blood in the city (v. 13). Now these leaders stagger through the streets defiled, driven away with the leper’s cry, “Away! Unclean!”, unwelcome even among the nations, and the face of the LORD himself has scattered them (vv. 14–16).
verseByVerse.theology: Those who lead God's people bear the heaviest responsibility, and the judgment fell hard on the leaders.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD gave full vent to his wrath; he poured out his hot anger, and he kindled a fire in Zion that consumed its foundations. The kings of the earth did not believe, nor any of the inhabitants of the world, that foe or enemy could enter the gates of Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD poured out his anger in full and burned Zion to its foundations, though no one on earth had believed Jerusalem could fall.

The LORD gave full vent to his wrath. For centuries God had been slow to anger, sending prophet after prophet. Now the anger is poured out, and the fire reaches the foundations, as Moses had sung: “a fire is kindled by my anger… and sets on fire the foundations of the mountains” (Deuteronomy 32:22).

The kings of the earth did not believe. Jerusalem had withstood the Assyrians in Hezekiah’s day, and everyone assumed it could not fall, its own people most of all, who trusted in “the temple of the LORD” (Jeremiah 7:4).

None of it is left over. There is another place where God’s wrath was given full vent, the one that matters most. At the cross God put his Son forward “as a propitiation by his blood” (Romans 3:25), the sacrifice that bears and turns away wrath. Jerusalem’s fire burned for a season and left survivors. The wrath that fell on Christ was spent in full, so that for those who trust him none is left over.

In everyday life. No city, church, nation or person is too established to fall if it abandons God. The sense of being untouchable is itself one of the signs of danger.

verseByVerse.quote: This was for the sins of her prophets and the iniquities of her priests, who shed in the midst of her the blood of the righteous. They wandered, blind, through the streets; they were so defiled with blood that no one was able to touch their garments. "Away! Unclean!" people cried at them. "Away! Away! Do not touch!" So they became fugitives and wanderers; people said among the nations, "They shall stay with us no longer." The LORD himself has scattered them; he will regard them no more; no honor was shown to the priests, no favor to the elders.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The city fell for the sins of its prophets and priests, who shed righteous blood, and now these leaders are driven out like lepers and scattered by the LORD himself.

The sins of her prophets. Now the poet names the root. The men who should have spoken for God and led worship had become the chief offenders: they had “shed in the midst of her the blood of the righteous”. Jeremiah himself was nearly killed by them: “the priests and the prophets and all the people laid hold of him, saying, ‘You shall die!’” (Jeremiah 26:8).

Away! Unclean! The men who had pronounced others unclean, now stained with the blood they shed, are treated as unclean themselves. The law required a leper to “cry out, ‘Unclean, unclean’” and to live alone “outside the camp” (Leviticus 13:45–46). Now the priests and prophets are driven off with that cry, and not even the nations will have them.

The LORD himself has scattered them. The ESV notes that the Hebrew says ‘The face of the LORD’, a heartbreaking phrase for a priest to hear. The priests had been commanded to bless the people with the words “the LORD make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you” (Numbers 6:25). Now the face of the LORD has scattered them.

Six centuries later. Jesus stood in the same city and spoke to its religious leaders of “all the righteous blood shed on earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah” (Matthew 23:35). Within days the priests had handed over the Righteous One himself.

The Holy One made himself the outcast. When a leper knelt before Jesus, “he stretched out his hand and touched him” (Mark 1:41). And Jesus himself “suffered outside the gate”, driven out like an unclean thing, “in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Hebrews 13:12). The Holy One made himself the outcast so that outcasts could be made clean. And the blessing the priests lost he brings back: God “has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6).

For those who lead. Religious leaders have a unique power to do harm, because they do it in God’s name. That is why Scripture judges them so strictly, and why every pastor and teacher should tremble.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–20 — A Nation Which Could Not Save
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Every saviour but God failed at the moment he was needed. The people watched the horizon until their eyes gave out, waiting for a nation that could not save them (v. 17). Meanwhile the hunters closed in: they could not walk in their own streets, and pursuers swifter than eagles chased them over the mountains and lay in wait in the wilderness (vv. 18–19). Last of all the king of David’s line, “the breath of our nostrils”, under whose shadow they had hoped to live, was caught in the enemy’s pits (v. 20). Every human hope has run out, which clears the way for the word of hope that follows.
verseByVerse.theology: Every saviour but God fails at the moment he is needed, even the king of David's line.

verseByVerse.quote: Our eyes failed, ever watching vainly for help; in our watching we watched for a nation which could not save. They dogged our steps so that we could not walk in our streets; our end drew near; our days were numbered, for our end had come. Our pursuers were swifter than the eagles in the heavens; they chased us on the mountains; they lay in wait for us in the wilderness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people wore out their eyes watching for a nation that could not save them, while the enemy hunted them down and left them nowhere to run.

Our eyes failed. During the siege the people watched the horizon for help, above all from Egypt. An Egyptian army did march out, and the Babylonians drew back for a while, but then it went home (Jeremiah 37:5–7). They watched until their eyes gave out, for “a nation which could not save”.

Swifter than the eagles. Moses had warned of a nation “swooping down like the eagle” (Deuteronomy 28:49); Jeremiah said, “his horses are swifter than eagles” (Jeremiah 4:13). When the wall was breached and the king and his soldiers fled by night toward the Arabah, the Babylonians caught them in the plains of Jericho (Jeremiah 39:4–5). There was nowhere to run from a judgment God had sent.

In everyday life. Every one of us has an Egypt, something we look to for rescue instead of God: a relationship, a career, a savings account, a political leader, a medical treatment. Some of these are good gifts, but none of them can save. “Put not your trust in princes, in a son of man, in whom there is no salvation” (Psalm 146:3). “There is salvation in no one else” but Christ (Acts 4:12).

verseByVerse.quote: The breath of our nostrils, the LORD's anointed, was captured in their pits, of whom we said, "Under his shadow we shall live among the nations."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their last hope, the king of David’s line on whom their life seemed to depend, was caught in the enemy’s pits.

The LORD’s anointed. This is King Zedekiah, the last of the kings of David’s line to reign in Jerusalem. The Babylonians captured him, killed his sons before his eyes, blinded him and took him to Babylon in chains (2 Kings 25:6–7).

The breath of our nostrils. The people called him “the breath of our nostrils”, as necessary as air, and hoped to live “under his shadow”. Zedekiah was a weak and faithless king, but he sat on David’s throne, and God had promised that “David shall never lack a man to sit on the throne” (Jeremiah 33:17). When he was dragged off, it looked as though the promise to David had died with him.

A righteous Branch. It had not. Jeremiah had spoken of a coming “righteous Branch” for David, whose name would be “The LORD is our righteousness” (Jeremiah 23:5–6).

The true Anointed was also captured. The psalm had said, “The kings of the earth set themselves… against the LORD and against his Anointed” (Psalm 2:2), and the apostles saw it happen in Jerusalem, where Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel gathered “against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed” (Acts 4:26–27). He too was seized and handed over to foreign rulers. But he rose, and he reigns. Zedekiah could not be the shelter his people hoped to live under; Christ can: “He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High will abide in the shadow of the Almighty” (Psalm 91:1).
verseByVerse.note: “The LORD’s anointed” is King Zedekiah, captured as he fled.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The cup of wrath does not stay with God’s people forever, and those who gloat over their fall will drink it in turn. Edom, Israel’s brother nation, which cheered as Jerusalem fell, is told with bitter irony to rejoice while it can, for the cup will pass to it and leave it drunk and exposed (v. 21). Then comes the first clear word of hope since chapter 3: “The punishment of your iniquity, O daughter of Zion, is accomplished”, and God will keep her in exile no longer. Edom’s sins, by contrast, will be uncovered and punished (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: The cup of wrath does not stay with God's people forever; for them the punishment has an end.

verseByVerse.quote: Rejoice and be glad, O daughter of Edom, you who dwell in the land of Uz; but to you also the cup shall pass; you shall become drunk and strip yourself bare. The punishment of your iniquity, O daughter of Zion, is accomplished; he will keep you in exile no longer; but your iniquity, O daughter of Edom, he will punish; he will uncover your sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Edom, which gloated over Jerusalem’s fall, will drink the same cup of wrath, but for Zion the punishment is complete and the exile will end.

O daughter of Edom. Edom was Israel’s brother nation, descended from Esau, the brother of Jacob (Genesis 25:30). When Jerusalem fell, Edom cheered and helped. The psalmist remembered: “Remember, O LORD, against the Edomites the day of Jerusalem, how they said, ‘Lay it bare, lay it bare, down to its foundations!’” (Psalm 137:7), and Obadiah condemned it: “do not gloat over the day of your brother in the day of his misfortune” (Obadiah 12). The poet places her “in the land of Uz”, a region probably east or south-east of Judah, best known as Job’s homeland (Job 1:1) and linked with Edom elsewhere (Genesis 36:28; Jeremiah 25:20–21).

To you also the cup shall pass. “Rejoice and be glad” is bitter irony. The cup of God’s wrath, which Jeremiah was told to make the nations drink, with Edom named among them (Jeremiah 25:15, 21), will come round to Edom too: “As you have done, it shall be done to you” (Obadiah 15).

Is accomplished. Then, suddenly, a word of hope: the punishment is “accomplished”, and it will not go on forever. It is the message God gave through Isaiah: “cry to her that her warfare is ended, that her iniquity is pardoned” (Isaiah 40:2).

It is finished. The word looks beyond the return from Babylon. In Gethsemane Jesus prayed, “let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26:39), and then he drank it. On the cross he said, “It is finished” (John 19:30).

Two destinies. Here are the two destinies of the whole human race. For Zion the punishment is accomplished; for Edom the sins are uncovered, that is, exposed and punished. The difference is not how bad Zion had been, for on one reading of verse 6 her iniquity was greater than Sodom’s. The difference is that God had bound himself to her by covenant, and in Christ he binds himself to everyone who comes to him.

Do not gloat. No one should gloat over another’s fall under God’s judgment: the same cup is passed around the whole world, and the only question is whether someone else has drunk it for you. The Germans have a word for what Edom felt, Schadenfreude, joy at someone else’s misfortune, and our culture has made a spectator sport of it. A celebrity is exposed or a rival caught out, and the reaction arrives within minutes, gleeful and certain. Why does it feel so good? Because another person’s fall lets us feel taller without having to grow. Jesus told of a man who stood in the temple and prayed, “God, I thank you that I am not like other men” (Luke 18:11); his whole religion rested on the comparison, and the irreligious version is the same, only louder. Scripture will not let us enjoy it, and not because it pretends the fallen are innocent: Edom’s cup did come round. It is because the only one who ever had the right to look down on sinners came down among them instead, and was himself mocked as he hung on the cross (Mark 15:29–32). Once you have seen that, the person on the floor is no longer someone worse than you. He is someone who needs what you were given.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that “he will keep you in exile no longer” may also be read ‘he will not exile you again’. Either way, God has set an end to Zion’s exile.
verseByVerse.note: Uz here is linked with Edom, which gloated over Jerusalem’s fall.

4.title: How the Gold Has Grown Dim
4.overview:
Where we are. After the hope of chapter 3, the fourth poem goes back down into the siege and what it did to people. Like chapters 1 and 2 it is an alphabetic acrostic, one verse to each letter of the Hebrew alphabet.

The message. Sin had turned Zion’s gold into clay and its tenderness into cruelty, and the men who should have led the people to God bore the heaviest guilt. Every human saviour failed, from Egypt to the king of David’s line. Yet the God who punished has set a limit: the punishment of Zion’s iniquity is accomplished, while those who gloat over her will drink the same cup.

Why it was said. The survivors carried memories almost too terrible to speak of, and questions with them: how could the city everyone thought could never fall have fallen, who was to blame, and would the punishment ever end? And Edom, their brother nation, was cheering (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. First the poet makes us look: the precious sons of Zion are treated as clay pots, children beg for bread, princes shrivel, and the punishment outweighs Sodom’s, down to mothers who ate their own children, as Moses had warned (vv. 1–10). Then he names the cause: the LORD poured out his anger, and it fell for the sins of the prophets and priests who shed righteous blood, now driven out like lepers (vv. 11–16). The people confess how they watched in vain for a nation that could not save, while the hunters closed in and the LORD’s anointed king was captured (vv. 17–20). At last the poem turns: Edom will drink the cup in her turn, but Zion’s punishment is accomplished, and her exile will end (vv. 21–22).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need the chapter exposes, by pattern and by promise. The priests failed and the king of David’s line was captured, leaving no one to stand between the people and God and no shelter to live under. Christ is both the true priest, who suffered outside the gate to make the unclean clean (Hebrews 13:12), and the true Anointed, seized and handed over to foreign rulers yet raised to reign. The cup that passes round the nations he drank in Gethsemane, and the punishment chapter 4 calls accomplished he finished on the cross: “It is finished” (John 19:30).

For us. No church or person is too established to fall, and those who lead God’s people are the most answerable. Stop looking to Egypts that cannot save, and refuse the pleasure of gloating over anyone’s fall. For all who are in Christ, the punishment of their iniquity has been fully borne.
4.theology:
A person's worth before God does not change when the world treats him as worthless (vv. 1-2; Isa 43:4; 1 Pet 1:18-19).

Sin's consequences reach into the most natural affections God created, even a mother's love; the covenant curses were fulfilled exactly as Moses warned (vv. 3-4, 10; Deut 28:56-57).

The more a people has been given, the more it must answer for: Jerusalem’s judgment exceeded Sodom’s (v. 6; Ezek 16:48; Matt 11:23-24; Luke 12:48).

Religious leaders who abuse their office and silence the righteous bear heavy guilt (v. 13; Jer 26:8; Matt 23:35).

Every saviour other than God fails, whether foreign allies or a king of David's line (vv. 17, 20; Ps 146:3). God's promise to David did not die with Zedekiah; it was fulfilled in Jesus, the Anointed who was captured and rose (Jer 23:5-6; Acts 4:26-27).

The cup of wrath passes to every nation, but for God's covenant people the punishment has an end. In Christ it has been fully borne: it is finished (vv. 21-22; Isa 40:2; Matt 26:39; John 19:30).
4.examples:
The poem's images are hard to forget: pure gold that has somehow tarnished, young men worth their weight in gold treated like cheap clay pots, a jackal feeding her young when a mother cannot, and children once dressed in purple clinging to a rubbish heap, their faces so changed that neighbours no longer know them.

Priests who once pronounced others unclean are driven off with the cry Unclean! The people watch the horizon for an army that turns back, and the king they called the breath of their nostrils is dragged away in chains. Then, at the very end, comes the word no one expected: the punishment is accomplished.

keyVerse.quote: The punishment of your iniquity, O daughter of Zion, is accomplished; he will keep you in exile no longer
keyVerse.note: After a whole poem of horror, this is the first clear word of hope since chapter 3: the punishment has a limit, set by God, and it is complete. It looks beyond the return from Babylon to the word spoken from the cross, “It is finished” (John 19:30). For all who belong to Christ, the punishment of their iniquity has been fully borne.

4.reflection:
Verses 1–2 describe people worth their weight in gold being treated like cheap clay pots. Where do you see people treated as disposable today, and how should the price God paid for his people (1 Peter 1:18–19) change the way you treat them?

Verse 13 lays the city’s fall at the door of its prophets and priests. Why does Scripture judge religious leaders so strictly? How can we pray for faithful leaders, and how should we respond when leaders fail?

The people watched for “a nation which could not save” (v. 17). What are the “Egypts” you are tempted to look to for rescue instead of God?

Edom gloated over Jerusalem’s fall (v. 21). Why is enjoying another’s downfall so tempting, and how does the cross take away our right to it?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Look, and See Our Disgrace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s people may bring the concrete details of their distress to him and ask him to act. The last poem is a prayer from the whole community: “Remember, O LORD, what has befallen us; look, and see our disgrace!” (v. 1). Then they lay out what life under occupation has become: the family land handed to strangers, homes without fathers, water and firewood that must be bought, and pursuers who allow no rest (vv. 2–5). They hold out their hands to foreign powers for bread, live with the damage of their fathers’ sins, and are ruled by slaves (vv. 6–8). Even food is gathered at the risk of life, and famine burns in their bodies (vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.theology: God's people may bring the concrete details of their distress to him and ask him to remember.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember, O LORD, what has befallen us; look, and see our disgrace! Our inheritance has been turned over to strangers, our homes to foreigners.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole community asks the LORD to remember them and see their disgrace, for the land he gave them has been handed over to strangers. From the first verse to the last, this prayer says “we”, “us” and “our”.

Remember, O LORD. When the Bible asks God to remember, it is not reminding him of something he has forgotten, but asking him to act on what he knows. When God remembered Noah, the waters went down (Genesis 8:1); when “God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant”, the exodus began (Exodus 2:24).

Our inheritance has been turned over to strangers. The land had never been Israel’s to sell: “the land is mine. For you are strangers and sojourners with me” (Leviticus 25:23). Now the inheritance he gave, family by family, has been handed to others, and other people live in the houses their grandparents built.

Jesus, remember me. A dying thief made the same prayer beside Jesus, “Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23:42), and he was heard that very day (Luke 23:43). No one is too far gone to pray it.

A different inheritance. Christians are given an inheritance that cannot be turned over to strangers: “an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you” (1 Peter 1:4). Houses can be lost; what God keeps for his people cannot.
verseByVerse.note: Chapter 5 has 22 verses but is not an acrostic (its verses do not begin with the letters of the alphabet in order): it is a prayer rather than a lament.

verseByVerse.quote: We have become orphans, fatherless; our mothers are like widows. We must pay for the water we drink; the wood we get must be bought. Our pursuers are at our necks; we are weary; we are given no rest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without fathers to protect them, forced to buy what was once free and hounded without rest, the people feel orphaned, even before God.

We have become orphans, fatherless. With many men dead or in exile, the families left behind had no one to protect them, and deeper still the people feel fatherless before God himself. Yet God calls himself “Father of the fatherless and protector of widows” (Psalm 68:5).

We must pay for the water we drink. Water and wood from their own land now had to be bought from the occupiers. At the beginning God had given them “cisterns that you did not dig, and vineyards and olive trees that you did not plant” (Deuteronomy 6:11). They received everything free and treated it as theirs by right; now they pay for water.

We are given no rest. They are tired, and no one lets them stop. It is the curse Moses had described: “among these nations you shall find no respite” (Deuteronomy 28:65). Weariness without rest is a picture of life under sin.

What grace gives away. The night before he died, Jesus said to his friends, “I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you” (John 14:18): no one who belongs to Christ is ever truly an orphan. God still offers freely what sin made them pay for: “Come, buy wine and milk without money and without price” (Isaiah 55:1). And the one who can end the weariness has said, “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). Sin makes us pay for what grace gives away.

verseByVerse.quote: We have given the hand to Egypt, and to Assyria, to get bread enough. Our fathers sinned, and are no more; and we bear their iniquities. Slaves rule over us; there is none to deliver us from their hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Begging foreign powers for bread and ruled by slaves, the people live with the damage of their fathers’ sins, yet do not hide behind them.

We have given the hand to Egypt. To give the hand was to make a pact or to submit. For years Judah had turned to Egypt and Assyria for security, and Jeremiah had asked, “what do you gain by going to Egypt to drink the waters of the Nile? Or what do you gain by going to Assyria to drink the waters of the Euphrates?” (Jeremiah 2:18). Now they hold out their hands to foreign powers simply to eat.

We bear their iniquities. Sin’s consequences do pass down the generations; God himself said he visits “the iniquity of the fathers on the children” (Exodus 34:7). The generation that caused the ruin was mostly dead, and their children were living in it. But read on to verse 16: “woe to us, for we have sinned!” They carry consequences they did not start, and they confess sins they have committed themselves; so must we, lamenting the damage we inherit and owning our own sin. Ezekiel had to correct exiles who blamed their fathers’ sins in order to deny their own (Ezekiel 18:2–4).

Slaves rule over us. Servants of a foreign power now order them about, and “there is none to deliver”. That is the condition of every person under sin: “everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin” (John 8:34), and the slave cannot free himself.

Bread, freedom and a sin-bearer. Every soul goes looking for bread somewhere, and only one place gives enough: “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger” (John 6:35). To slaves comes the gospel: “So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed” (John 8:36). And of the Servant of the LORD it is said, “he shall bear their iniquities” (Isaiah 53:11): the iniquities we inherited and the iniquities we added, he carried.

Uncertain wording. Assyria had fallen some twenty-five years before Jerusalem, so it is not certain what “Assyria” means here. It may look back to the fathers’ old alliances (v. 7), or it may be an old name for whatever power ruled Mesopotamia, which now meant Babylon. Either way, the people had looked to the great powers for bread and safety and found neither.

verseByVerse.quote: We get our bread at the peril of our lives, because of the sword in the wilderness. Our skin is hot as an oven with the burning heat of famine.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even gathering food risks death, and famine burns in their bodies, and they bring these bodily details to God in prayer.

At the peril of our lives. Going out to gather food meant risking raiders in the open country, so every meal cost a risk to someone’s life, and those at home burned with the fever of famine. These are real people with real bodies.

In everyday life. Prayer like this is not unspiritual. God invites his people to tell him exactly what is wrong: the price of water, the danger of the fields, the fever in the body. Jesus taught us to pray, “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matthew 6:11). Nothing that concerns your life is too ordinary to bring to God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Behind every loss the people come back to the one cause they can confess: we have sinned. The prayer names the worst of the occupation without softening it: women raped, princes hung up, elders despised, young men and boys forced into slave labour, the city gate empty of counsel and the streets empty of music (vv. 11–14). Joy has gone and dancing has turned to mourning (v. 15). Then comes the confession: “The crown has fallen from our head; woe to us, for we have sinned!” (v. 16). What makes them heartsick most of all is not their own hardship but Mount Zion, the place of God’s presence, lying desolate with jackals prowling over it (vv. 17–18).
verseByVerse.theology: Behind every loss the people come back to the one cause they can confess: we have sinned.

verseByVerse.quote: Women are raped in Zion, young women in the towns of Judah. Princes are hung up by their hands; no respect is shown to the elders. Young men are compelled to grind at the mill, and boys stagger under loads of wood. The old men have left the city gate, the young men their music.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prayer names the worst cruelties of the occupation without softening them: women raped, princes hung up, elders despised, the young enslaved, and the city emptied of wisdom and joy.

Women are raped in Zion. The Bible names this. It does not soften it or look away, and neither should we. Rape was, and still is, a weapon of war. That the verse stands in Scripture matters for every woman who has suffered this: God has seen it and written it into his own book as an outrage, neither hidden from him nor unimportant to him. “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit” (Psalm 34:18).

Princes are hung up by their hands. The law said, “a hanged man is cursed by God” (Deuteronomy 21:23), and the princes of Judah were hung up in public disgrace. The elders, whom the law commanded to be honoured (“You shall stand up before the gray head and honor the face of an old man”, Leviticus 19:32), are treated with contempt.

Young men are compelled to grind at the mill. Turning the millstone was the work of servants and prisoners; when the Philistines captured Samson, “he ground at the mill in the prison” (Judges 16:21). The strength of Judah’s young men is spent in slave labour, and even boys are loaded down like pack animals.

The old men have left the city gate. The gate was where the elders sat to settle disputes and give counsel; now no one sits there. The young men used to play music; now there is none. Wisdom and joy have both gone out of the city, and a community without the counsel of its old and the songs of its young has lost its life.

The curse borne. Paul quotes the law about the hanged man when he explains the cross: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). The Prince of Peace was hung up too, so that the curse on his people could end.

If this has happened to you. The church, which carries this book, must be a place where such suffering can be spoken of and is met with compassion, not silence. If you have been raped or sexually abused, it was not your fault, and the shame is not yours. Seek safety and help, tell someone you trust, and report it to the police, with someone beside you if that helps; if you are in danger now, call the emergency services.

Uncertain wording. “By their hands” may mean that the princes were hung up by their own hands, as torture or as a display of the dead, or that they were hanged by the enemy’s hand. Either way, Judah’s leaders were put to open shame.

verseByVerse.quote: The joy of our hearts has ceased; our dancing has been turned to mourning. The crown has fallen from our head; woe to us, for we have sinned! For this our heart has become sick, for these things our eyes have grown dim, for Mount Zion which lies desolate; jackals prowl over it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joy has turned to mourning and the crown has fallen, and at last the people name the cause, “we have sinned”, grieving most of all for the desolate place of God’s presence.

Our dancing has been turned to mourning. It is the exact reverse of the psalm: “You have turned for me my mourning into dancing” (Psalm 30:11). Sin turned dancing into mourning, and only God can turn it back. Through Jeremiah he had promised to: “Then shall the young women rejoice in the dance, and the young men and the old shall be merry. I will turn their mourning into joy” (Jeremiah 31:13). The very losses in these verses, young women, young men, the old, dancing and joy, are the ones God named in his promise.

The crown has fallen from our head. The crown, their glory as God’s people, lies in the dust. And here at last, after all the lament, the prayer names the reason. No blaming Babylon, no blaming the fathers: “we have sinned”. This is where every road back to God begins: “Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy” (Proverbs 28:13).

For Mount Zion which lies desolate. Of all the losses, this one makes them heartsick: Mount Zion, where God put his name, is desolate. Jeremiah had said God would make Jerusalem “a heap of ruins, a lair of jackals” (Jeremiah 9:11), and now wild animals walk where the priests used to minister.

A crown that cannot fall. The one who wore a crown of thorns gives his people a crown that cannot fall: “Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life” (Revelation 2:10). And the New Testament tells believers, “you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem” (Hebrews 12:22). The Zion that jackals prowl was never the final one.

What grieves you most? They grieve most not for their comfort but for the place of God’s presence, a good test of any heart.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–22 — But You, O LORD, Reign Forever
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Everything on earth has fallen, but one throne has not, and so the people dare to pray. “But you, O LORD, reign forever” (v. 19) is the ground of the whole prayer. Because he reigns, the question is sharper: why has he forgotten them so long (v. 20)? They ask him to restore them, not first to the land but to himself, for only he can turn them back, and to renew their days as of old (v. 21). The book ends on an open fear, “unless you have utterly rejected us” (v. 22): a question only God can answer, and his answer, given in his promises and at last in Christ, is that he does not utterly reject his people.
verseByVerse.theology: The book ends on a question only God can answer, and his answer is that he does not utterly reject his people.

verseByVerse.quote: But you, O LORD, reign forever; your throne endures to all generations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every earthly throne has fallen, but the LORD’s throne stands forever, and that is the ground of all their hope.

But you, O LORD, reign forever. Everything in the first eighteen verses has fallen, and here the prayer looks up. David’s throne in Jerusalem is gone; the LORD’s is not. “But you, O LORD, are enthroned forever; you are remembered throughout all generations” (Psalm 102:12).

The ground under everything. If God still reigns, then what happened was not beyond his control, and what comes next is not beyond his power. When everything you built has come down, this is the sentence to hold on to.

The throne belongs to the Lamb. The New Testament shows whose throne it is: “of the Son he says, ‘Your throne, O God, is forever and ever’” (Hebrews 1:8). At the end of the Bible, in the new Jerusalem, stands “the throne of God and of the Lamb” (Revelation 22:3). The throne that endures to all generations belongs to the Lamb who was slain.

verseByVerse.quote: Why do you forget us forever, why do you forsake us for so many days? Restore us to yourself, O LORD, that we may be restored! Renew our days as of old— unless you have utterly rejected us, and you remain exceedingly angry with us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because God reigns, the people ask why he has left them so long, beg him to bring them back to himself, since only he can, and end with an honest fear that he may have rejected them for good.

Why do you forget us forever? Because God reigns forever, the question becomes sharper, not softer: if you are King, why have you left us so long? It is the language of the psalms: “How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever?” (Psalm 13:1). And God had already answered it through Isaiah. “Zion said, ‘The LORD has forsaken me; my Lord has forgotten me.’” And God replied, “Can a woman forget her nursing child… Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you. Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands” (Isaiah 49:14–16).

Restore us to yourself. Not first to the land or to prosperity, but to God, for the deepest loss was never the city. And they know they cannot turn themselves around: if they are to come back, God must bring them back. It is Ephraim’s prayer in Jeremiah, “bring me back that I may be restored, for you are the LORD my God” (Jeremiah 31:18), and the psalm’s, “Restore us, O God; let your face shine, that we may be saved!” (Psalm 80:3).

Renew our days as of old. Not simply turn the clock back, but make new: “if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation” (2 Corinthians 5:17).

Unless you have utterly rejected us. So the book ends not with an answer but with a fear: unless it is too late, unless you have finished with us. It is a startling way to end a book of the Bible, and it is deliberate: Lamentations does not tidy grief up, but leaves the question hanging, because that is how grief really feels, and because the answer does not lie in the people’s feelings but in God. (When the book is read in the synagogue, verse 21 is read again after verse 22, so that the reading does not end on that fear.)

God had already answered. “I will not spurn them, neither will I abhor them so as to destroy them utterly and break my covenant with them” (Leviticus 26:44). “If the heavens above can be measured, and the foundations of the earth below can be explored, then I will cast off all the offspring of Israel” (Jeremiah 31:37). Paul asked the same question centuries later: “has God rejected his people? By no means!” (Romans 11:1).

Christ forsaken and rejected. There was one who was truly forsaken. On the cross Jesus cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46), so that God could say to all who are in him, “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5). He was utterly rejected (Mark 8:31) and bore the exceeding anger of God, and because he did, he can make a promise that closes the question at the end of Lamentations for everyone who comes to him: “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37).

The heart of grace. Repentance is something we do, and it is also something God gives, by the Spirit who gives “a new heart” (Ezekiel 36:26): “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44). If you want to come back to God and find you cannot make your heart do it, pray this prayer. It is the prayer he answers.

Uncertain wording. The opening words of verse 22 are a Hebrew phrase that can mean ‘unless’, ‘but’ or ‘even if’, so translations differ. Some take the verse as a fearful condition, as the ESV does; others as a statement (‘but you have utterly rejected us’) or as a question (‘or have you utterly rejected us?’). However it is read, the people are still speaking to God, which they would not do if they believed he had finished with them.

5.title: Remember, O LORD
5.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 4 ended with the first clear word of hope; now, in the book’s last poem, the whole community stops describing and starts praying. The poem keeps twenty-two verses, like the acrostics before it, but lets go of the alphabet (see the introduction).

The message. Stripped of land, freedom, leaders and joy, God’s people bring the whole truth of their misery and of their sin to the LORD, because he still reigns. They ask him to bring them back to himself, since they cannot turn themselves, and they leave their deepest fear open before him. When faith has nothing left, it still prays, and that prayer is the one God answers.

Why it was said. The survivors in Judah were living under foreign rule: their land and homes held by strangers, water and wood sold back to them, food gathered at the risk of their lives, and no king or temple left (see the introduction). Many feared that God had finished with them for good.

How the chapter makes its case. The prayer asks God to remember and see, and lays out in plain detail what occupation has meant: the inheritance lost, families fatherless, water bought, hands held out to foreign powers, the fathers’ sins still bearing fruit, and bread won at the peril of life (vv. 1–10). Then it names the worst, women raped, princes hung up, the young enslaved, the gate and the music silent, until the confession comes: “The crown has fallen from our head; woe to us, for we have sinned!” (vv. 11–18). Finally the prayer looks up: “But you, O LORD, reign forever” (v. 19). So the people ask why he has forgotten them, pray, “Restore us to yourself, O LORD, that we may be restored!”, and end on an honest fear, “unless you have utterly rejected us” (vv. 19–22).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the need the chapter exposes and by the character of God revealed in him. The people cannot restore themselves; God must bring them back, and in Christ he does. The throne that endures to all generations belongs to the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 22:3). The fear on which the book ends, utter rejection, was borne by the Son, who cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46), so that he can promise, “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37).

For us. Bring God the plain details of your trouble, however ordinary or dark. Confess your own sin rather than hiding behind others. And when you cannot make your heart return, pray this prayer, “Restore us to yourself”, to the King who still reigns and never casts out those who come.
5.theology:
To ask God to remember is to ask him to act on his covenant (v. 1; Gen 8:1; Exod 2:24; Luke 23:42).

Sin's consequences pass down the generations, yet each generation must confess its own sin; the Servant of the LORD bore the sins we inherited and the sins we added (vv. 7, 16; Exod 34:7; Ezek 18:2-4; Isa 53:11).

Scripture does not hide the violence done to the weak; God sees it and records it as an outrage (vv. 11-13; Ps 34:18).

When every earthly throne falls, the LORD's throne endures, and it is the throne of God and of the Lamb (v. 19; Ps 102:12; Heb 1:8; Rev 22:3).

Restoration is first restoration to God himself, and it is God's gift: he must turn his people if they are to be turned (v. 21; Jer 31:18; Ps 80:3; John 6:44).

God does not utterly reject his people (v. 22; Lev 26:44; Jer 31:37; Rom 11:1-2). Christ was rejected so that no one who comes to him will ever be cast out (Mark 8:31; John 6:37).
5.examples:
The prayer is made of ordinary losses: paying for water from your own well, holding out your hand to a foreign power for a loaf, an empty city gate where no music plays, and jackals walking where the priests once ministered.

In the middle stands a crown in the dust and the plain words we have sinned. Above it all stands one throne that has not fallen: But you, O LORD, reign forever. A people who cannot turn themselves ask God to turn them, and the book ends with unless, a question the Saviour answers.

keyVerse.quote: Restore us to yourself, O LORD, that we may be restored!
keyVerse.note: The book’s last request asks for what the people most need and cannot do for themselves: to be brought back to God himself. It rests on verse 19, for only the LORD who reigns forever can restore. In Christ, who was rejected so that no one who comes to him will be cast out (John 6:37), God has answered this prayer for all who pray it.

5.reflection:
The people tell God in plain detail what life has become (vv. 1–10), from the price of water to the fever of famine. What keeps you from bringing the ordinary details of your troubles to God in prayer?

Verse 7 says “we bear their iniquities”, but verse 16 says “we have sinned!” How do we hold together the damage we inherit from others and responsibility for our own sin, and how does Christ answer both?

Verse 19 sets God’s everlasting throne against everything that has fallen. What has fallen in your life or world that makes this verse precious, and how does knowing that the throne belongs to the Lamb (Revelation 22:3) change the way you pray?

The book ends with a fear: “unless you have utterly rejected us” (v. 22). How does Jesus’ promise in John 6:37 answer it, and who do you know who needs to hear that answer?
